rationale: A model has already seen its fitting data, so strong performance there may just reflect noise it has memorised, which is why you test elsewhere. Fitting data is not by nature smaller, it is not error-free, and performance on it is perfectly measurable, just not trustworthy as a judge.

stem: Interpretability of a model refers to:
options: how many predictors the model happens to contain in total once fitted
how accurately the model predicts on data that it has not previously seen
how quickly the model can be re-run once a fresh batch of data arrives
how readily a person can follow why the model gave a particular output
rationale: Interpretability is how easily a person can follow the reasoning behind an output. Accuracy on unseen data is generalisation, speed of re-running is a computational matter, and the count of predictors is not the same as how interpretable the model is.

stem: A risk model reports that a group of patients each has a 20 percent chance of an event. Over time, almost exactly 20 percent of them have the event. This is evidence of good:
options: external validation, carried out on a genuinely different population
discrimination, since the cases have been ranked in the correct order
calibration, since the stated probabilities match the observed rate
sensitivity of the output to the assumptions the model was built on
rationale: Stated probabilities matching observed rates is good calibration. Discrimination is about ordering cases rather than the accuracy of the numbers, external validation concerns a different population, and sensitivity concerns how output responds to changed assumptions.

stem: An analyst re-runs a forecast several times, each time changing one key assumption about future demand, to see how far the projected budget moves. This is best described as:
options: a sensitivity analysis of the forecast against its assumptions
external validation of the forecast on a different population
cost allocation spread across the various lines of the budget
calibration of the probabilities the forecast happens to report
rationale: Varying an assumption and watching the output move is a sensitivity analysis. Calibration concerns whether probabilities mean what they say, external validation concerns a different population, and cost allocation concerns splitting shared costs.

stem: A model performs well when tested on held-back data from the same source, and a team now wants to know whether it holds on a genuinely different population elsewhere. They are moving from:
options: underfitting towards overfitting
sensitivity analysis towards cost allocation
internal validation towards external validation
calibration towards discrimination
rationale: Testing on held-back data from the same source is internal validation; checking a genuinely different population is external validation. The other pairs name unrelated moves: calibration to discrimination, sensitivity to allocation, and underfitting to overfitting.

stem: The reason interpretability can matter as much as accuracy is that:
options: the accuracy of a model simply cannot be measured at all unless the model is interpretable
models that are interpretable have no further need of any validation once they are built
a model whose workings cannot be interrogated may carry hidden bias into a decision
an interpretable model is reliably more accurate than a more opaque one on the same task
rationale: An uninterrogable model can carry hidden bias that lands unequally, which is why interpretability can matter as much as accuracy. Interpretable models are not always more accurate, accuracy can be measured without interpretability, and interpretable models still need validation.

stem: Saying a model's purpose decides what is left out means that:
options: a model should retain the full set of available variables so as to stay objective
the intended purpose of a model becomes relevant once it has already been built
leaving features out of a model tends to reduce how useful that model can be
the objective determines which features of reality a model keeps and which it sets aside
rationale: A model is built for a purpose, and that purpose governs what it keeps and what it drops. Keeping every variable is not what purpose-driven simplification means, purpose guides the build from the start rather than afterwards, and leaving things out is how a model becomes useful rather than a flaw.

stem: Describing models as opinionated is a way of saying that:
options: a model embeds choices about what matters, so it is not a neutral mirror of the data
models are best avoided in decisions because they cannot ever be made objective
a model reflects the data exactly, with no choices made by the analyst at all
a model's output is a matter of personal opinion rather than a form of evidence
rationale: Models are opinionated in that they embed choices about what counts, so they are never neutral mirrors. That is not the same as reflecting the data with no choices, nor does it make output mere opinion, nor does it argue against using models at all.

stem: Two analysts model the same deaths-and-population data, one using a crude rate and one an age-standardised rate. The difference illustrates that:
options: one of the two rates involved must simply have been calculated the wrong way
a structural choice about what to hold constant shifts what the model shows
the choice between the two rates has no real bearing on the conclusion drawn
the age structure of a population is not relevant to a mortality comparison
rationale: Choosing a crude or an age-standardised rate is a structural choice about what to hold constant, and it changes what the model shows. Neither rate is wrong, the choice clearly does affect the conclusion, and age is plainly relevant to comparing mortality.

stem: When a model reports that a predictor and an outcome move together, the careful reading is that:
options: the predictor in question has been shown to cause the outcome being modelled
the association is firm proof that the two are in fact unrelated in the world
the model is showing an association, which need not amount to a causal link
the relationship has to hold in each and every individual case within the data
rationale: A model showing two things moving together is showing an association, which need not be causal. It does not establish cause, it certainly does not show the two are unrelated, and a population-level association need not hold in every individual.

stem: Treating uncertainty honestly when interpreting a model's output means:
options: presenting the output as a range of plausible values rather than one exact figure
discarding any model output that happens not to be stateable with full certainty
reporting only the single most likely value, so as not to confuse the eventual reader
treating a wider band of uncertainty as firm proof that the model has gone wrong
rationale: Honest interpretation presents output as a range of plausible values rather than one exact number. Reporting only a point estimate hides the uncertainty, discarding uncertain output throws away usable information, and a wide range reflects genuine uncertainty rather than proving the model wrong.

stem: A commissioner reads a model output as saying that more green space causes lower obesity, when the model has only shown the two are related across areas. The interpretive error is:
options: confusing a fixed cost with a variable cost in a costing model
mistaking a model's calibration for its discrimination instead
treating an interaction between predictors as multicollinearity
reading an association as though it were established causation
rationale: Reading a shown association as proven cause is the error here. The other options name mistakes from different parts of the field: calibration versus discrimination, fixed versus variable cost, and interaction versus multicollinearity, none of which is what has gone wrong.

stem: A team needs a model of patient flow to decide where a bottleneck sits, and deliberately leaves out detail on individual clinical histories. Leaving that detail out is:
options: a calibration problem in the model's outputs
a flaw, since a model should include all available detail
a defensible structural choice driven by the model's purpose
evidence the model is overfitted to the data
rationale: Leaving out detail that the purpose does not need is a defensible structural choice, not a defect. A model need not include all detail, omitting detail is not overfitting, which concerns chasing noise, and it is not a calibration problem, which concerns whether reported figures mean what they say.

stem: Two valid models of the same system give somewhat different projections because each represents the system slightly differently. The soundest interpretation is that:
options: the disagreement is proof that neither of the two models can be trusted in any respect
one of the two models has to be straightforwardly wrong and so ought to be discarded
the two sets of projections should simply be averaged to make the disagreement go away
different structural choices can give different outputs, so the assumptions need stating
rationale: Different defensible representations can give different outputs, so the assumptions behind each need to be stated and weighed. It does not follow that one is simply wrong, that neither can be trusted, or that blindly averaging them is the right move.

stem: The quality-adjusted life year is best described as a measure that:
options: weights future health benefits below present ones to reflect timing
values a health outcome purely by the number of life-years it adds
expresses a health gain as its cost per unit of benefit
combines length of life and quality of life into a single figure
rationale: A QALY combines how long a person lives with the quality of that time, so a year in full health scores higher than a year in poor health. The life-years-only reading ignores quality and describes unadjusted life-years. The cost-per-unit reading describes an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, not the QALY itself. The weighting-of-future-benefits reading describes discounting.

stem: A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) represents:
options: the average number of years a patient survives after treatment
a year of life adjusted for the quality of health during it
a year of life gained, regardless of the health experienced in it
the monetary value placed on a year of a person's life
rationale: A QALY combines length of life with the quality of health during that time, so a year in poor health counts as less than a year in full health. A year of life gained regardless of quality is an unadjusted life-year, which is the length axis only. A monetary value on a year of life is a cost figure, not a QALY. Average survival after treatment is a life-expectancy measure with no quality adjustment.

stem: An incremental cost-effectiveness ratio expresses:
options: the financial return that is generated for each pound that is invested in a programme
the share of a budget that a new programme would consume in its first year
the extra cost per additional unit of health gained when moving from one option to another
the total cost of a programme divided by the number of people it treats
rationale: An ICER is a comparison between two options: the difference in cost divided by the difference in effect, so it reads as extra cost per extra unit of health. The total-cost-per-person reading is an average cost, not an incremental one. The share-of-budget reading describes budget impact. The return-per-pound reading describes return on investment.

stem: A team reports that a new pathway costs an extra 8,000 pounds and yields an extra 0.4 QALYs compared with current care, and divides one by the other. The figure they have produced is:
options: an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio comparing the new pathway with current care
the budget impact of adopting the new pathway across the service
an average cost-effectiveness ratio calculated for the new pathway taken entirely on its own
the net present value of switching to the new pathway
rationale: Dividing the difference in cost by the difference in effect between two options gives an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, which is exactly what the team has done. An average ratio would divide one option's total cost by its total effect, with no comparison. Net present value would discount and sum costs and benefits over time, not form a ratio. Budget impact would estimate the total affordability of adoption, not cost per QALY.

stem: In economic evaluation, the opportunity cost of committing resources to a programme is:
options: the additional cost incurred each time the programme expands by one unit
the cost that has already been spent and cannot now be recovered
the total amount of money that the programme requires in order to run over each year
the value of the benefit forgone by not using those resources in their next-best alternative
rationale: Opportunity cost is the benefit given up from the next-best use of a resource, which is why it matters when budgets are fixed. The total-money-required reading describes the financial or budgetary cost. The cost-per-extra-unit reading describes marginal cost. The already-spent reading describes a sunk cost.

stem: Discounting is applied in economic evaluation because:
options: costs shared across programmes must be divided by the number of programmes
costs and benefits occurring further in the future are valued less than those occurring now
benefits that are uncertain must be reduced in proportion to their risk
future costs must instead be increased to allow for the expected annual rate of general price inflation
rationale: Discounting reflects time preference: a cost or benefit in the future counts for less than the same one today, so future values are scaled down. The inflation reading confuses discounting with an inflation adjustment, which is a separate correction. The risk reading describes adjusting for uncertainty, not timing. The dividing-shared-costs reading describes cost apportionment.

stem: Discounting and adjusting for inflation differ in that discounting:
options: converts all future prices into their equivalent value in a chosen base year's currency
corrects for the falling purchasing power of money over time
applies only to costs and leaves health benefits untouched
reflects a preference for benefits sooner rather than later, regardless of any price changes
rationale: Discounting captures time preference, the idea that sooner is worth more than later, and applies even when prices are stable. The falling-purchasing-power reading and the base-year-currency reading both describe inflation adjustment. The costs-only reading is wrong because discounting is applied to both future costs and future health benefits.

stem: A positive net present value for a proposed investment indicates that:
options: its discounted benefits exceed its discounted costs over the chosen time horizon
its benefits exceed its costs before any discounting is applied
it can be funded quite comfortably from within the current financial year's revenue budget
it produces health gains at a lower cost per QALY than the comparator
rationale: Net present value sums discounted costs and benefits, so a positive figure means discounted benefits outweigh discounted costs across the horizon. The before-discounting reading omits the discounting that defines NPV. The current-year funding reading describes affordability or budget impact. The lower-cost-per-QALY reading describes cost-effectiveness against a comparator.

stem: A prevention programme prevents few events in its first two years but many over twenty. An evaluation using only a two-year time horizon would most likely:
options: overstate the benefits by counting gains that have not yet happened
convert the benefits into a generic utility measure automatically
understate the programme's benefits by stopping before most of them accrue
remove the need to discount because the period is short
rationale: A time horizon sets the window over which costs and benefits are counted; ending it at two years cuts off the later gains, so the benefits are understated. The overstating reading has the direction backwards. The no-discounting reading is wrong because a short horizon still involves discounting, just over fewer years. The utility-measure reading confuses the horizon with the choice of outcome measure.

stem: In HM Treasury Green Book appraisal, the appraisal period for an option should be set to:
options: a length that captures the costs and benefits relevant to the decision
the point at which the option's own spending stops
the length of the current spending review period
the expected working life of the main piece of capital equipment involved
rationale: The appraisal period should be long enough to capture the costs and benefits that matter for the decision. In practice the Green Book uses ten years as a standard default, but that is a starting point rather than a rule: it is extended where benefits accrue over a longer period, as with prevention or long-lived infrastructure, and shortened where effects are short-lived. Tying the period to the spending review fixes it to a funding cycle rather than to when benefits fall. Using the asset's working life captures the capital but not benefits that continue beyond it. Stopping when spending stops ignores benefits that continue after the costs end.

stem: The opportunity cost of a decision differs from its financial cost in that opportunity cost:
options: counts only the cash costs that happen to fall within the current financial year
rises each time the chosen option is expanded by one more unit
captures the value of the best alternative given up, which may not appear in any budget
records the cash actually paid out to run the chosen option
rationale: Opportunity cost is the value of the forgone next-best alternative, and that lost benefit need not show up as a cash line in any budget. The cash-paid-out reading describes the financial cost. The current-year reading describes an in-year budgetary cost. The rises-with-expansion reading describes marginal cost.

stem: A generic measure such as the QALY is useful across different programmes mainly because it:
options: reflects the severity of a condition better than a disease-specific scale
counts the number of people treated by each programme on a like-for-like basis
allows health gains from unlike conditions to be compared on a common scale
captures effects on length of life that condition-specific measures leave out
rationale: A generic outcome measure puts gains from unlike conditions on one scale, so a hip programme and a mental health programme can be compared. Capturing length of life is something disease-specific measures can also do, so that is not what makes the QALY generic. Reflecting severity within a single condition is a job a disease-specific scale often does better. Counting people treated is a measure of activity, not of health gain.

stem: The defining feature of a cost-benefit analysis is that it:
options: values costs in money and benefits in a natural clinical unit
values both costs and benefits in money, so the two can be set against each other directly
reports only the total first-year cash cost of adopting a new programme into service
values benefits in a generic utility measure such as the QALY
rationale: Cost-benefit analysis puts benefits as well as costs into monetary terms, allowing a direct net-benefit comparison. The money-and-clinical-unit reading describes cost-effectiveness analysis. The utility-measure reading describes cost-utility analysis. The first-year-cost reading describes budget impact.

stem: In a cost-effectiveness analysis, the health outcome is expressed as:
options: a distinct monetary value placed directly on the overall size of the health benefit produced
a generic utility measure combining length and quality of life
the share of the budget the intervention would take up
a natural clinical unit, such as cost per case detected or per life-year gained
rationale: Cost-effectiveness analysis measures outcomes in natural clinical units, giving results like cost per case detected. The monetary-value reading describes cost-benefit analysis. The generic-utility reading describes cost-utility analysis. The share-of-budget reading describes budget impact.

stem: A cost-utility analysis differs from a cost-effectiveness analysis in that its outcome measure is:
options: a monetary valuation placed directly on the size of the health benefit produced
a generic utility measure such as the QALY, combining length and quality of life
a single natural clinical unit specific to the condition
the number of people the programme can treat within budget
rationale: Cost-utility analysis uses a generic utility measure such as the QALY, which is what lets it compare across conditions. The natural-clinical-unit reading describes cost-effectiveness analysis. The monetary-valuation reading describes cost-benefit analysis. The number-treated reading describes a capacity or budget-impact question.

stem: The main difference between cost-benefit analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis lies in:
options: whether the analysis considers more than one option
how the benefits are valued, in money for one and in natural units for the other
how the costs themselves are valued, since one of them does not count its costs in money at all
whether discounting is applied to future values
rationale: The two methods differ in how benefits are valued: money in cost-benefit analysis, natural units in cost-effectiveness analysis. The costs reading is wrong because both value costs in money. The discounting reading is wrong because both discount future values. The more-than-one-option reading is wrong because both compare options.

stem: A cost-utility analysis is generally preferred over a cost-effectiveness analysis when:
options: the programmes being compared produce different kinds of health outcome
the programmes being compared share a single natural outcome measure
the health benefits can readily be valued in money
the outcome of interest is the number of deaths prevented
rationale: Cost-utility analysis uses a generic measure such as the QALY, so it suits programmes whose outcomes differ in kind. When the programmes share one natural outcome, cost-effectiveness analysis already works and the generic measure is not needed. When benefits can be valued in money, cost-benefit analysis fits. When the outcome is deaths prevented, that is itself a natural unit, so cost-effectiveness analysis suffices.

stem: An analysis values both the costs and the health benefits of an option in money and compares the two. This type of analysis is:
options: cost-benefit analysis
cost-effectiveness analysis
budget impact analysis
cost-utility analysis
rationale: Valuing both costs and benefits in money and setting them against each other is cost-benefit analysis. Cost-effectiveness analysis measures the outcome in a natural clinical unit rather than money. Cost-utility analysis measures it in a generic utility such as the QALY. Budget impact analysis looks at affordability, not at benefits valued in money.

stem: An analysis measures an option's outcome in a natural clinical unit, such as cost per case detected. This type of analysis is:
options: budget impact analysis
cost-benefit analysis
cost-utility analysis
cost-effectiveness analysis
rationale: Measuring the outcome in a natural clinical unit such as cost per case detected is cost-effectiveness analysis. Cost-utility analysis uses a generic utility measure such as the QALY instead. Cost-benefit analysis values the outcome in money. Budget impact analysis addresses affordability rather than the outcome per unit of cost.

stem: A finance lead asks not whether a new drug is good value but simply whether the system can pay for it next year. The analysis this calls for is:
options: cost-effectiveness analysis
budget impact analysis
cost-utility analysis
cost-benefit analysis
rationale: The question is affordability, not value, so budget impact analysis is the right tool. Cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analysis both answer value-for-money questions, which is explicitly not what was asked. Cost-benefit analysis also addresses value, by putting benefits and costs in money.

stem: Cost-effectiveness analysis is a natural choice when the options being compared:
options: need only a check that they fit within next year's budget
produce different kinds of outcome that must be compared on a common scale
all produce the same kind of outcome, measurable in one shared natural unit
have benefits that are easiest to express directly in money
rationale: Cost-effectiveness analysis works when a single natural unit, such as cases detected, fits all the options being compared. The different-outcomes-on-a-common-scale reading is the case for cost-utility analysis. The benefits-in-money reading points to cost-benefit analysis. The fit-within-budget reading points to budget impact.

stem: A commissioner must choose between funding a hip replacement service and a smoking cessation service from one budget. The evaluation method that lets these be compared directly is:
options: cost-effectiveness analysis
cost-utility analysis
budget impact analysis
return on investment
rationale: The two services produce quite different outcomes, so a generic utility measure is needed to compare them, which is cost-utility analysis. Cost-effectiveness analysis fails here because there is no natural unit shared by mobility and quitting smoking. Budget impact analysis would tell you affordability, not which offers more health. Return on investment would compare financial returns, not health gain across the two.

stem: A recognised strength of cost-benefit analysis, which is also its main difficulty, is that it:
options: places a monetary value on health benefits, which allows wide comparison but is hard to do credibly
reports only the affordability of a programme within the budget
expresses outcomes in natural clinical units that need no valuation step
avoids discounting altogether by holding every one of its values in present-day money terms
rationale: Cost-benefit analysis values benefits in money, which lets it compare across very different areas but raises the hard problem of pricing health credibly. The natural-clinical-unit reading describes cost-effectiveness analysis, which avoids monetary valuation. The avoids-discounting reading is wrong because cost-benefit analysis still discounts. The affordability reading describes budget impact.

stem: Discounting is applied to costs and benefits that fall in future years mainly because:
options: estimates further into the future are less certain than near-term ones
prices tend to rise over time, so future amounts buy less
future costs and benefits are harder to attribute to the option
value received sooner is generally preferred to the same value received later
rationale: Discounting reflects time preference: a given cost or benefit is worth more now than later, so future values are scaled down. Rising prices describe inflation, which is handled separately by working in real terms. Greater uncertainty about distant estimates is dealt with through sensitivity and scenario analysis, not the discount rate. Difficulty of attribution is an evaluation-design issue, not the reason for discounting.

stem: A time-series approach to forecasting produces its projection by:
options: following a defined group forward as its members age
extending patterns found in a run of past observations of the same measure
combining projected births, deaths and migration into a population total
converting projected need into the service activity it would generate
rationale: Time-series forecasting works from a sequence of past values of one measure and projects their pattern forward. Combining births, deaths and migration describes a demographic component projection. Following a defined group as it ages describes cohort-based forecasting. Converting need into activity describes service-demand forecasting.

stem: Trend extrapolation differs from a fuller time-series model in that it:
options: fits an explicit statistical model and reads uncertainty from it
simply projects the direction of the past trend forward, without modelling its components
separates the series into its seasonal and underlying components before projecting it
adjusts the projection for expected changes in the population's age structure
rationale: Trend extrapolation just carries the observed direction of travel forward, without decomposing the series. Separating out seasonal and underlying components is what a fuller time-series model does. Fitting an explicit model and quantifying its uncertainty is also a property of the fuller approach, not of plain extrapolation. Adjusting for age structure brings in demographic drivers that simple extrapolation does not use.

stem: Using demographic drivers in a forecast means basing the projection on:
options: alternative assumptions set deliberately high and low
changes in disease incidence, prevalence and risk factors
the observed statistical pattern in a run of past values
changes in the size and age structure of the population over time
rationale: Demographic drivers are population features such as size and age structure, and a forecast built on them projects from how those change. The disease-change reading describes epidemiological drivers. The statistical-pattern reading describes a time-series approach. The high-and-low-assumptions reading describes scenario modelling.

stem: Epidemiological drivers in a forecast are inputs such as:
options: the seasonal and cyclical patterns in a series of past observations
the birth rate, ageing and net migration together shaping the whole population's structure
the incidence, prevalence and risk-factor trends of the conditions of interest
the high, central and low variants used to bound a projection
rationale: Epidemiological drivers concern disease: incidence, prevalence and risk factors and how they move. The birth-rate-and-ageing reading describes demographic drivers. The seasonal-patterns reading describes time-series structure. The high-central-low reading describes scenario variants.

stem: Cohort-based forecasting differs from a whole-population trend forecast in that it:
options: assumes the age structure of the population stays fixed over time
follows defined groups forward so their needs change as they age
relies only on the recent trend in the overall figure
projects a single aggregate total for the whole population at once
rationale: Cohort-based forecasting tracks defined groups as they age, so age-specific needs shift over the projection. Projecting one aggregate total for the whole population is the whole-population approach it is being contrasted with. Relying only on the recent overall trend describes simple extrapolation. Assuming a fixed age structure is the opposite of what a cohort approach does, since ageing is the point of it.

stem: A planning team converts a projected rise in the number of people with diabetes into the number of clinic appointments the service will need. This is best described as:
options: trend extrapolation
cohort-based forecasting
service-demand forecasting
time-series forecasting
rationale: Turning projected need into the service activity required is service-demand forecasting. Trend extrapolation would carry a past appointments trend forward rather than derive activity from projected prevalence. Cohort-based forecasting would follow a defined group as it ages, which is not what the team has done. Time-series forecasting would project from a past run of the appointments figure itself.

stem: The main risk in relying on trend extrapolation is that:
options: it cannot be applied to data collected over successive years
the forecast fails when the conditions that produced the past trend change
it requires following individual cohorts through the whole period
it can be used only when the particular outcome of interest is measured directly in money
rationale: Trend extrapolation assumes the past trend continues, so it goes wrong when the underlying conditions shift. The measured-in-money reading invents a constraint that belongs to economic valuation, not forecasting. The following-cohorts reading confuses it with cohort-based forecasting. The cannot-apply-to-yearly-data reading is simply false, since time trends are exactly its input.

stem: A forecast built on demographic drivers projects future need mainly from:
options: changes in the rates at which people use services
changes in the incidence and prevalence of disease
changes in the resources available to provide care
changes in the size and age structure of the population
rationale: Demographic drivers are population features such as size and age structure, so a demographic forecast projects from how those change. Incidence and prevalence of disease are epidemiological drivers, a separate input. Rates of service use are utilisation patterns, downstream of need. Available resources are a supply constraint, not a driver of underlying need.

stem: Cohort-based forecasting is a particularly good fit when future need depends on:
options: how a defined group's needs change as its members grow older
a short-term trend that is expected to continue unchanged
the total size of the population rather than its age make-up
seasonal peaks and troughs within each year
rationale: Cohort-based forecasting suits questions where need turns on a defined group ageing over time. A short-term trend expected to hold is better handled by extrapolation. Need driven by total population size rather than age make-up does not require following cohorts. Seasonal within-year variation is a time-series feature, not a cohort one.

stem: A planner wants to project future need for a service by following successive age groups as they move through the population over the next twenty years. The most suitable forecasting approach is:
options: service-demand forecasting
cohort-based forecasting
time-series forecasting
trend extrapolation
rationale: Following successive age groups through the population over time is exactly what cohort-based forecasting does. Trend extrapolation would simply carry a past trend forward without tracking age groups. Time-series forecasting would project from a past run of the aggregate figure. Service-demand forecasting would translate need into activity, which is a later step, not the age-tracking projection itself.

stem: Population ageing is expected to change health and care need mainly by:
options: increasing the number of people living with long-term and multiple conditions
increasing demand for maternity and early-years services
concentrating need into a small number of acute infectious disease outbreaks
reducing need overall as birth rates fall
rationale: An older population carries more long-term and co-occurring conditions, so need rises and shifts towards chronic care. More demand for maternity and early-years services would follow a younger, growing population, not an ageing one. Concentration into acute infectious outbreaks describes a different epidemiological pattern. A fall in birth rates affects population growth but is not how ageing itself changes the pattern of need.

stem: Multimorbidity as a driver of health and care need refers to:
options: the total number of separate conditions present across a population
the spread of an infectious condition through a community
the presence of two or more long-term conditions in the same person
a single long-term condition that worsens gradually over time
rationale: Multimorbidity is two or more long-term conditions co-occurring in one person, which complicates care. The total-across-a-population reading describes overall disease burden, not co-occurrence in individuals. The single-condition reading omits the co-occurrence that defines multimorbidity. The spread-through-a-community reading describes transmission of infection.

stem: The prevalence of a long-term condition in a population is:
options: the average number of years people live after diagnosis
the number of people living with the condition at a given time
the number of new cases arising over a defined period
the rate at which the condition leads to death
rationale: Prevalence counts everyone living with the condition at a point or over a period, the stock of cases. The new-cases reading describes incidence. The leads-to-death reading describes a mortality or case-fatality measure. The years-after-diagnosis reading describes survival.

stem: The incidence of a condition is best described as:
options: the proportion of cases that end in recovery
the total number of people still at risk who have not yet developed the condition
the total number of existing cases present at one time
the rate at which new cases arise in a population over a period
rationale: Incidence is the rate of new cases arising over a period. The existing-cases reading describes prevalence. The proportion-recovering reading describes an outcome or recovery rate. The at-risk-not-yet-affected reading describes the population at risk, the denominator, not incidence itself.

stem: A condition's yearly rate of new cases has held steady, yet the number of people living with it keeps rising. The most likely explanation is that:
options: the condition is being diagnosed more often than before
new cases of the condition are being detected earlier than they used to be
the population at risk of the condition is growing
people are surviving longer with the condition, so cases accumulate
rationale: With steady incidence, prevalence rises when people live longer with the condition, so cases build up in the population. Earlier detection shifts when a case is counted but does not by itself raise the standing number living with it. A growing at-risk population would tend to raise the count of new cases too, yet incidence is stated as steady. More frequent diagnosis would show up as higher recorded incidence, which is also ruled out.

stem: The prevalence of a long-term condition tends to rise when:
options: new cases stop arising but recovery rates also fall to zero
the population at risk shrinks while case numbers stay fixed
people live longer with the condition, so cases accumulate in the population
the condition instead becomes rapidly and reliably fatal fairly soon after its onset
rationale: Prevalence rises when people live longer with a condition, adding to the pool of existing cases. The new-cases-stop reading describes a static or falling stock, not a rise. The shrinking-at-risk-population reading would tend to lower counts, not raise prevalence. The rapidly-fatal reading would cut prevalence by shortening survival.

stem: Two areas have a similar prevalence of a condition but quite different rates of hospital admission for it. Looking at service utilisation patterns would mainly help to:
options: value the health outcomes each area's service produces
establish which of the two areas has the more accurate prevalence estimate
show how similar levels of need are translating into different use of services
measure how many new cases each area is seeing per year
rationale: Utilisation patterns show how need turns into actual use of services, which is exactly what differs between the two areas here. Deciding which prevalence estimate is more accurate is a data-quality question, not a utilisation one. Counting new cases per year is measuring incidence. Valuing health outcomes is an economic-evaluation step, not a look at utilisation.

stem: Modelling need by adding up single conditions tends to understate the need of multimorbid patients because:
options: patients with several conditions tend to use services less than expected
each condition is usually less severe when it occurs alongside others
conditions occurring together are generally counted twice in the data
their conditions interact, so combined need is more than the sum of the parts
rationale: In multimorbidity, conditions interact and complicate care, so combined need exceeds a simple sum of the separate conditions. Conditions being less severe together would, if anything, reduce need, which is the wrong direction. Multimorbid patients tend to use more services, not fewer. Double-counting in the data would overstate rather than understate need, so it does not explain the gap.

stem: A district finds both a growing share of over-75s and more people carrying several conditions at once. For long-term need, the most likely combined effect is:
options: need rises faster than population growth alone would suggest, as ageing and multimorbidity compound
need is unaffected, since ageing and multimorbidity cancel each other out
need rises exactly in step with the growth in total population size
need falls away overall because older people concentrate their care into fewer, larger episodes
rationale: Ageing and multimorbidity reinforce each other, so need grows faster than headcount alone implies. The in-step-with-population reading ignores the change in the mix of need. The falls-because-fewer-episodes reading contradicts the higher care load of multimorbidity. The cancel-each-other reading has no mechanism and is not the case.

stem: When planning the capacity a service needs for people currently living with a condition, the more relevant measure is:
options: incidence, since it counts only the brand-new cases arising this year
prevalence, since it counts all those living with the condition who may need care
the case-fatality rate, since it shows how many die from the condition
the at-risk population, since it instead counts everyone who might develop it only later
rationale: Planning capacity for current patients turns on prevalence, the count of everyone living with the condition. Incidence captures only new cases and would understate the caseload. The case-fatality rate describes deaths among cases, not care demand. The at-risk population counts people who might develop the condition, not those who have it.

stem: Aligning investment decisions to the planning cycle matters because:
options: funding and commitments have to fit the timing of budget-setting and planning rounds
it guarantees that any early intervention will always pay back within one year
it converts capital spending into revenue spending automatically
it removes the need to discount benefits that fall in future years
rationale: Investment has to fit the rhythm of budget-setting and planning rounds, or decisions miss their window. The removes-discounting reading confuses planning timing with economic discounting. The converts-capital-to-revenue reading invents an accounting effect. The guarantees-payback reading is not something a planning cycle can promise.

stem: Programme budgeting and marginal analysis (PBMA) supports resource allocation mainly by:
options: showing where moving resources between areas of spend would add most benefit
checking that each programme has spent within its allocation
forecasting how demand for each programme will change over time
setting the total budget that is available to each programme for the year
rationale: PBMA maps current spend across areas and uses marginal analysis to find where shifting resources yields more benefit. Setting the total budget for each programme is a funding decision that PBMA informs but does not perform. Forecasting future demand is a separate modelling task. Checking spend against allocation is budget monitoring, not marginal analysis.

stem: The marginal analysis element of resource allocation asks:
options: what extra benefit the next unit of spending would produce, and where it is greatest
what monetary value should be placed on a full programme's benefits
what proportion of the cases in a population will eventually end in recovery
what the total cost of running all current programmes comes to
rationale: Marginal analysis looks at the benefit from the next unit of resource, guiding where an extra pound does most good. The total-cost reading describes overall programme budgeting, not the marginal step. The monetary-value reading describes cost-benefit valuation. The proportion-recovering reading is an epidemiological outcome measure, not an allocation question.

stem: A commissioner funds a programme that treats a condition early, accepting higher spending now to avoid larger costs and worse outcomes later. The investment rationale being applied is:
options: discounting
opportunity cost
budget impact
early intervention
rationale: Spending earlier to head off later cost and harm is the early intervention rationale. Opportunity cost concerns the forgone next-best use of the money, not the timing of spend. Budget impact asks about affordability now, not the early-versus-late trade. Discounting adjusts future values but is not itself a reason to intervene early.

stem: The distinction between capital and revenue spending matters for investment decisions because:
options: capital spending never requires any ongoing running costs afterwards
revenue spending is always recovered in full once again within the same financial year
the two are funded and controlled differently, so a plan must use the right kind for each cost
the two are interchangeable, so either can cover any cost as needed
rationale: Capital and revenue are governed and funded on different rules, so a plan has to match each cost to the right type. The revenue-always-recovered reading is untrue. The capital-never-needs-running-costs reading ignores the revenue consequences that follow capital investment. The interchangeable reading denies the very distinction the item is about.

stem: Marginal analysis in resource allocation is concerned with:
options: the additional benefit gained from the next unit of resource spent
the average benefit per pound across a programme as a whole
the benefit forgone by not funding a programme at all
the total benefit produced by a programme across all its spending
rationale: Marginal analysis looks at the benefit from the next unit of resource, guiding where an extra pound does most good. Total benefit across all spending is an aggregate figure, not a marginal one. Average benefit per pound smooths over the margin that the analysis is about. Benefit forgone from not funding at all is an opportunity-cost idea, not the marginal step.

stem: Buying a new scanner is classed as capital rather than revenue spending because it:
options: is expected to reduce the service's running costs in future
will be paid for out of next year's budget rather than this year's
purchases a physical asset that will be used over several years
is a large enough sum to need sign-off from senior management
rationale: Capital spending buys a lasting asset used over several years, which is what the scanner is. The size of the sum and who signs it off do not determine the capital-revenue split. Which year's budget pays for it is a timing matter, not the basis of the classification. An expected fall in running costs is a benefit of the purchase, not the reason it counts as capital.

stem: The longer-term resource argument for early intervention rests on the idea that:
options: spending now avoids the need to discount any future benefits
treating later removes any need to plan across more than one single budget year
acting earlier can lower the total need and cost that would otherwise build up later
earlier action always works out cheaper than later action in every case
rationale: Early intervention is argued for on the basis that acting sooner reduces the larger need and cost that would accumulate later. The cheaper-in-every-case reading overstates a case that depends on the condition. The avoids-discounting reading confuses the timing argument with discounting. The treating-later-removes-planning reading is backwards, since later treatment does not simplify multi-year planning.

stem: Scenario modelling differs from sensitivity analysis in that scenario modelling:
options: varies one input at a time to see how much the result moves
reports one single central estimate with a stated margin of error around it
checks the model against outturn data once the future is known
builds out several internally consistent sets of assumptions about the future
rationale: Scenario modelling constructs whole coherent futures, each a consistent set of assumptions, and compares them. Varying one input at a time is sensitivity analysis, the thing it is being contrasted with. Reporting a single central estimate with a margin is a point forecast, not a set of scenarios. Checking against outturn data is validation, done after the fact.

stem: Building a set of best-case, worst-case and policy scenarios is intended to:
options: show the range of plausible outcomes and how a chosen policy shifts them
test whether the model's code runs without technical error
pick out the one scenario most likely to occur and then discard the rest
express the forecast's outcomes only as a monetary net benefit
rationale: A scenario set maps the spread of plausible futures and shows how a policy choice moves them. The pick-one-and-discard reading defeats the purpose of holding several scenarios. The monetary-net-benefit reading describes cost-benefit analysis. The code-runs reading describes a technical check, not scenario purpose.

stem: Sensitivity analysis in a model is used to find out:
options: what the model itself actually predicts under its single central set of assumptions
how far the result changes when an uncertain input is varied across a plausible range
how much each programme actually costs to run over a full year
whether the population data used were collected accurately
rationale: Sensitivity analysis varies an uncertain input over a plausible range to see how much the result moves, showing which inputs matter most. The central-assumptions reading describes the base case, not the sensitivity test. The cost-to-run reading is a budgeting question. The data-collected-accurately reading concerns data quality, not sensitivity.

stem: A modeller presents not one figure but a range showing how the forecast moves as key inputs change. Compared with reporting a single point estimate, this mainly:
options: shows that the forecast has been checked against real outturn data
shows that the underlying model is free of coding errors
shows how sensitive the forecast is to the assumptions behind it
shows the monetary value of the forecast outcomes
rationale: Presenting a range as inputs change conveys how sensitive the forecast is to its assumptions, which a single figure hides. Being checked against outturn data is validation, a separate exercise. Freedom from coding errors is model verification, which a range does not demonstrate. Monetary value of outcomes is an economic-evaluation output, not what a sensitivity range shows.

stem: Structural uncertainty in a model refers to uncertainty in:
options: the model's form and the assumptions built into how it is put together
the quality of the raw data before it enters the model
the specific numerical values that are actually entered as the model's own inputs
the size of the budget available to run the modelling work
rationale: Structural uncertainty is about the model's form: the relationships and assumptions in how it is built. The numerical-values reading describes parameter uncertainty. The raw-data-quality reading describes a data issue, upstream of structure. The budget reading is unrelated to model uncertainty.

stem: Parameter uncertainty in a model refers to uncertainty about:
options: the quality of the raw data before it enters the model
the choice of structure and relationships in the model
the way the model's results are interpreted by users
the values assigned to the inputs the model uses
rationale: Parameter uncertainty concerns the values given to the model's inputs. The choice of structure and relationships is structural uncertainty, a different kind. The quality of the raw data is a data issue upstream of the parameters. How results are interpreted by users is a communication matter, not a source of model uncertainty.

stem: Two teams disagree: one is unsure whether the model should link the variables the way it does, the other is unsure what number to use for a key rate. Their two doubts are, respectively:
options: sampling uncertainty in both cases
parameter uncertainty and structural uncertainty
structural uncertainty and parameter uncertainty
calibration error and validation error
rationale: Doubt about how the model links its variables is structural uncertainty; doubt about the value of a rate is parameter uncertainty, so the order matches. The reversed option swaps the two. The calibration-and-validation reading names checking steps rather than the kinds of uncertainty described. The sampling-in-both reading forces one label onto two clearly different doubts.

stem: The difference between internal and external validation of a model is that internal validation checks:
options: how the model was funded, while external validation checks who actually built it
the model against a separate real-world dataset, while external validation checks its internal consistency
whether the input values are uncertain, while external validation fixes them
that the model behaves consistently within itself, while external validation compares it against independent data
rationale: Internal validation examines the model's own consistency and logic; external validation tests it against independent, real-world data. The reversed option swaps the two definitions. The funding-and-builder reading is unrelated to validation. The input-uncertainty reading confuses validation with uncertainty analysis.

stem: Selection bias is best described as a systematic error that arises when:
options: participants who leave before the study ends differ systematically from those who remain
those measuring the outcome are influenced by knowing which group a participant was in
one group receives extra care or attention beyond the intervention being evaluated
recruitment or allocation produces groups that already differ before any intervention
rationale: Selection bias is introduced at recruitment or allocation, when the groups being compared are not equivalent to begin with. Knowledge of allocation affecting measurement describes detection bias, unequal additional care describes performance bias, and systematic differences among those lost describes attrition bias.

stem: Performance bias refers to systematic differences between groups in:
options: the proportion of participants who complete the study in each arm
the care provided or behaviour that occurs alongside the intervention being studied
how the outcome is measured or judged once the study is under way
the characteristics that participants already have at the moment they enter the study
rationale: Performance bias concerns what happens to the groups during the study apart from the intervention itself, such as differences in co-interventions or in how participants are treated. Differences in outcome measurement point to detection bias, differences at entry point to selection bias, and differences in completion point to attrition bias.

stem: Detection bias is most likely to occur when:
options: more participants withdraw from one arm of the study than from the other
the two groups receive different amounts of clinical attention during follow-up
those assessing the outcome know which intervention each participant received
the randomisation sequence is predictable to the person enrolling participants
rationale: Detection bias arises when outcome assessment is influenced by awareness of group allocation, which blinding of assessors is designed to prevent. A predictable sequence relates to selection bias at allocation, unequal attention relates to performance bias, and differential withdrawal relates to attrition bias.

stem: Attrition bias is a concern in a study when:
options: participants lost to follow-up differ systematically from those who are retained
one group benefits from extra contact that the other does not receive
the people enrolling participants can foresee the next allocation
the outcomes are recorded differently depending on which group a participant is in
rationale: Attrition bias arises when loss to follow-up is related to the outcome or to group membership, so that those who remain are no longer comparable. Foreseeable allocation is a selection problem, group-dependent recording is detection bias, and unequal extra contact is performance bias.

stem: Internal validity refers to the extent to which a study:
options: recruits a sample large enough to detect a meaningful effect
measures the outcomes that matter most to patients and the public
produces findings that can be applied to other populations and settings
supports a sound causal conclusion for the conditions it actually studied
rationale: Internal validity is about whether the design and conduct of a study allow a trustworthy causal conclusion for the participants and setting examined. Applicability elsewhere is external validity, adequate sample size concerns statistical power, and measuring the right outcome is a separate matter of outcome selection.

stem: External validity is concerned with whether the findings of a study:
options: are precise enough to rule out a clinically trivial effect
hold for populations, settings or conditions beyond those directly studied
would be reproduced if the same study were repeated identically
reflect a genuine effect rather than chance or bias within the study
rationale: External validity, sometimes framed as applicability or transferability, asks whether results generalise beyond the studied sample and context. Whether the within-study effect is genuine is internal validity, exact repetition concerns reproducibility, and precision concerns the width of the confidence interval.

stem: In appraising qualitative research, 'credibility' broadly refers to whether:
options: enough participants took part to support statistical generalisation
the same themes would emerge if a different sample were studied
the study followed its published protocol without any deviation
the findings are a trustworthy interpretation of the participants' accounts
rationale: Credibility concerns whether the analysis genuinely reflects what participants conveyed, the qualitative counterpart to internal validity. Applicability to other samples is closer to transferability, statistical generalisation is not the aim of qualitative work, and protocol adherence is a separate procedural matter.

stem: The main reason for using a structured critical appraisal tool rather than an informal reading is to:
options: apply consistent, transparent criteria so appraisals can be compared and checked
establish whether the study's effect estimate reached statistical significance
convert the study's quality into a score that fixes its weight in any analysis
confirm that the study addressed a question relevant to the appraiser's setting
rationale: A structured tool sets out explicit criteria so different studies are appraised the same way and the judgement can be scrutinised by others. Checking statistical significance is one narrow question rather than the purpose, quality scoring to weight studies is a separate and debated practice, and judging relevance to a setting is a distinct step.

stem: Critical appraisal tools are typically design-specific because:
options: each design must be analysed with a different statistical test
the relevant outcome measure changes with the design
different designs are exposed to different forms of bias
journals require a specific named checklist for each design
rationale: Tools are tailored to a design because the threats to validity vary with how a study was built; a trial and a case-control study are not at risk of the same things. The choice of statistical test, journal requirements and outcome measure can vary too, but none of these is why appraisal is design-specific.

stem: Critical appraisal of a study is primarily concerned with:
options: how far the study's design and conduct support belief in its findings
how widely the study has since been cited by other researchers in the field
whether the findings agree with current clinical guidelines
whether the topic of the study is important to the field
rationale: Appraisal asks whether the way a study was done justifies trusting its results, independent of the headline finding. Agreement with guidelines, the importance of the topic and citation counts may all be of interest, but none of them tells you whether the study itself is sound.

stem: In an open-label trial of a physiotherapy programme, the clinicians who rated each patient's mobility at the end knew which patients had received the new programme. The most relevant risk this introduces is:
options: attrition bias
publication bias
detection bias
selection bias
rationale: Because outcome assessment depended on people who knew the allocation, the scoring could be swayed by that knowledge, which is detection bias and is guarded against by blinding assessors. Selection bias concerns how groups were formed, attrition bias concerns differential dropout, and publication bias operates across studies rather than within one.

stem: A 12-month trial of a weight-management service loses 40% of the intervention group and 12% of the control group to follow-up, and those who left tended to be the heaviest. The two arms were well matched at the start. The threat this poses to the findings is best described as:
options: detection bias
selection bias
attrition bias
performance bias
rationale: The groups were comparable at the start, but heavy differential loss linked to the outcome means those analysed at the end are no longer alike, which is attrition bias. Performance bias concerns care during the study, detection bias concerns outcome measurement, and selection bias concerns how the groups were formed at entry.

stem: The principal reason randomisation strengthens a controlled trial is that it:
options: ensures the sample is representative of the wider target population being studied
tends to distribute both known and unknown confounders evenly between the groups
removes the need to record participants' baseline characteristics
makes blinding of participants and assessors unnecessary
rationale: Random allocation works because, on average, it spreads confounding factors, including ones nobody has measured, across the arms, which is why trials can support causal claims. Representativeness comes from how the sample is drawn rather than how it is allocated, blinding remains important, and baseline characteristics are still recorded to check that balance was achieved.

stem: A cohort study is characterised by:
options: starting with people who already have the outcome and looking back at their exposures
measuring exposure and outcome together at a single point in time
assigning the exposure to participants and then following them forward
following groups defined by their exposure to see who later develops the outcome
rationale: A cohort study classifies people by exposure and follows them to observe outcomes over time. Starting from the outcome and looking back describes a case-control study, capturing both at once describes a cross-sectional study, and assigning the exposure describes a trial rather than an observational design.

stem: Case-control studies are particularly useful for:
options: measuring the absolute risk associated with an exposure
studying rare outcomes, or ones that take a long time to develop
estimating the incidence of a disease in the population
examining many different outcomes arising from a single exposure
rationale: By starting with cases, the design captures enough people with an uncommon or slow-developing outcome to study its exposures efficiently. Incidence and absolute risk need a defined population followed over time, which case-control sampling does not provide, and examining many outcomes from one exposure is a strength of cohort designs.

stem: A cross-sectional study is best suited to:
options: comparing earlier exposures in people with and without a condition
estimating how common a condition is at a single point in time
establishing whether an exposure came before the outcome
tracking the course of a disease over many years
rationale: Measuring exposure and outcome together gives a snapshot, which is ideal for prevalence but cannot show what came first. Establishing temporal order, following disease over time and comparing past exposures between cases and controls belong respectively to longitudinal, cohort and case-control approaches.

stem: Qualitative research is most appropriate when the aim is to:
options: understand the meanings, experiences or reasons behind people's behaviour
estimate the size of an effect together with its confidence interval
quantify how strongly an exposure and an outcome are associated
determine which of two treatments produces the better outcome
rationale: Qualitative work explores how and why, drawing out understanding that numbers alone cannot capture. The other aims all require effect sizes, measures of association or comparative outcome data, which are the province of quantitative designs.

stem: Traditional hierarchies of evidence rank study designs mainly according to their:
options: vulnerability to bias when estimating an intervention's effect
the number of participants they typically include
how recently the studies were published
the overall cost and the length of time needed to carry them out
rationale: Designs sit higher when their structure better protects an effect estimate from bias, which is why well-conducted trials usually outrank observational studies. Sample size, cost and recency may matter in other ways but are not what the hierarchy is ordering.

stem: A limitation of relying on the evidence hierarchy alone is that:
options: it assumes newer studies automatically replace older ones
it places qualitative research above trials for questions of effectiveness
the ranking depends on which journal publishes the study
a poorly conducted study can be less reliable than a sound one ranked below it
rationale: The hierarchy ranks designs in the abstract, but execution matters: a flawed trial can be beaten by a rigorous cohort study, so rank is a starting point not a verdict. Journal of publication does not set the rank, qualitative research is not ranked above trials for effectiveness, and the hierarchy makes no assumption that newer work supersedes older.

stem: In an observational study, a confounder is a factor that:
options: lies on the causal pathway that runs between the exposure and the outcome
is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the apparent association
is itself caused by both the exposure and the outcome together
is measured only after the outcome has occurred
rationale: A confounder is independently related to exposure and outcome and so creates a misleading association between them. A factor on the pathway is a mediator rather than a confounder, a factor caused by both is a collider, and timing of measurement alone does not define confounding.

stem: Observational studies are generally weaker than trials for causal questions mainly because they:
options: tend to follow their participants for shorter periods of time than trials do
are usually published in lower-ranking journals than trials
cannot exclude the possibility that unmeasured factors explain the association
depend on self-reported rather than objectively measured outcomes
rationale: Without randomisation, an observed association may be driven by confounders that were never measured, which is the core limitation for causal claims. Journal ranking is irrelevant to validity, observational studies can and do use objective outcomes, and many follow people for years, often longer than trials.

stem: A team wants to estimate how many adults in a town currently have undiagnosed high blood pressure. The most appropriate design is a:
options: case-control study
cross-sectional survey
randomised controlled trial
qualitative interview study
rationale: Estimating how common a condition is at one time is a prevalence question, which a cross-sectional survey answers directly. A case-control design starts from known cases, a trial evaluates an intervention, and qualitative interviews explore experience rather than measure prevalence.

stem: An observational study finds that people who drink more coffee have higher rates of lung cancer. Before accepting that coffee causes lung cancer, the first thing an appraiser should suspect is:
options: confounding, since coffee drinkers may differ in habits such as smoking
publication bias across the wider literature
detection bias in the way the cancer diagnosis was made and recorded
that the sample was too small for the result to hold
rationale: Smoking is associated both with coffee drinking and with lung cancer, so it can manufacture an association between them; this is the classic confounding example. Detection bias, sample size and publication bias are real concerns elsewhere, but none explains a spurious exposure-outcome link the way an unmeasured common cause does.

stem: A researcher wants to know whether smoking in pregnancy is associated with low birth weight. A randomised trial is not an option here mainly because:
options: smoking status changes too quickly to study
birth weight cannot be measured reliably
an outcome this common could not be detected within a trial
it would be unethical to assign people to a harmful exposure
rationale: You cannot ethically allocate pregnant women to smoke, so the exposure must be studied observationally, typically with a cohort design. Birth weight is readily measured, smoking can be ascertained, and a common outcome is easier, not harder, to study, so none of these is the reason a trial is ruled out.

stem: What most clearly distinguishes a systematic review from a traditional narrative review?
options: it is restricted entirely to evidence drawn from randomised controlled trials
it uses a predefined, explicit method for finding, selecting and appraising studies
it always presents its results as a pooled meta-analysis
it is commissioned and funded by a national body
rationale: The defining feature is a transparent, prespecified and repeatable process, so that the same search and selection could be reproduced by others. A systematic review need not include a meta-analysis, is not restricted to trials, and can be carried out by anyone, not only national bodies.

stem: Registering a systematic review protocol before starting the work mainly helps to:
options: secure funding for the review team
limit the scope for changing the methods once the results are seen
make the literature search quicker to carry out
increase the number of separate databases that have to be searched
rationale: A protocol fixed in advance makes it harder to adjust questions or outcomes after seeing the data, which protects against selective, results-driven choices. It is not primarily about search speed, funding or the number of databases, which are practical matters decided separately.

stem: PROSPERO is best described as:
options: a tool for grading the certainty of a body of evidence
a checklist for reporting completed systematic reviews
a database of published randomised controlled trials
an international register of systematic review protocols
rationale: PROSPERO is where review protocols are registered before the work begins, making the intended methods public. The reporting checklist is PRISMA, registers of trials are separate databases, and grading the certainty of evidence is what GRADE does.

stem: The PRISMA statement is primarily intended to:
options: assess the risk of bias present within each of the included studies
register the review's protocol in advance of the search
improve the transparency and completeness of how a review is reported
rank study designs in a hierarchy of evidence
rationale: PRISMA guides authors on what to report so a review can be understood and checked, including its flow of study selection. Registering the protocol is PROSPERO's role, judging within-study bias uses risk-of-bias tools, and ranking designs is the function of an evidence hierarchy.

stem: A systematic review aims to search several databases and sources rather than one mainly to:
options: meet a fixed rule that at least five databases are searched
lower the chance of missing relevant studies, which could bias the findings
make it more likely the review reaches the conclusion that was expected
increase the citation count of the finished review
rationale: Searching widely guards against an incomplete picture, since studies that are missed are often missed non-randomly and can skew the result. It is not done to inflate citations, to steer towards a desired conclusion, or to satisfy an arbitrary count of databases.

stem: Setting explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria before screening studies helps mainly by:
options: ensuring only studies with positive findings are kept in
reducing the number of separate databases that need to be searched
keeping study selection consistent and not shaped by the studies' results
fixing in advance how the results will be statistically pooled
rationale: Prespecified criteria mean studies are included or excluded on stated grounds rather than on whether their findings are liked, which protects against bias in selection. They do not exist to favour positive studies, to limit the search, or to determine the method of pooling, which is a separate decision.

stem: The flow diagram recommended for reporting a systematic review records:
options: the certainty of the evidence for each outcome
the number of records identified, screened, excluded and included
the pooled effect estimate and its confidence interval
the risk of bias that was judged for each of the included studies
rationale: The flow diagram traces how many studies moved through each stage from search to inclusion, with reasons for exclusion, so the process is transparent. Risk-of-bias judgements, the pooled estimate and the certainty rating are reported elsewhere, not in the flow diagram.

stem: When the studies in a systematic review are too different to combine statistically, the appropriate response is to:
options: pool them regardless, using a fixed-effect model
include only the single largest study and report its result alone
take a simple unweighted average of the study results
set out and synthesise the findings narratively rather than pooling
rationale: Where studies are too clinically or methodologically different, forcing a pooled number misleads, so a structured narrative synthesis is preferred. Reporting only the largest study, pooling regardless with a fixed-effect model, or taking a plain average all impose a single figure the evidence does not support.

stem: Two reviews of the same question reach opposite conclusions. One registered its protocol in advance and one did not. All else being equal, why might an appraiser place more trust in the registered review?
options: its methods and outcomes were set before the results could influence them
registration shows its literature search was more thorough
registered reviews are required to include a meta-analysis
registration means the studies it included were of higher quality
rationale: Prior registration reduces the room for outcome switching or after-the-fact changes, so the registered review's choices are less likely to have been steered by its findings. Registration says nothing in itself about search thoroughness, does not mandate a meta-analysis, and does not certify the quality of the studies included.

stem: A systematic review of a treatment includes only studies published in English. An appraiser should be concerned that this could:
options: affect only the time taken, not the conclusions reached
introduce bias if studies in other languages reached different conclusions
improve the review by keeping the included studies more consistent
make no difference, since most research appears in English anyway
rationale: Restricting by language can systematically omit relevant evidence, and if those omitted studies differ in their results the synthesis becomes biased. It is not made safe by the prevalence of English-language research, does not improve consistency in any meaningful sense, and bears on the findings, not merely the timing.

stem: A meta-analysis is:
options: a statistical combination of results from several studies
a narrative summary of all the literature published on a topic
a single large study designed to settle a question
a method for registering a review protocol
rationale: Meta-analysis pools quantitative results across studies to produce an overall effect with greater precision. A narrative summary does not combine results statistically, a single large study is not a synthesis of others, and registering a protocol is a separate step done on a register such as PROSPERO.

stem: Combining several studies in a meta-analysis can be valuable mainly because it:
options: corrects for bias in how the original studies were conducted
makes the result apply to populations that none of the studies examined
narrows the uncertainty around the overall effect by drawing on more data
gives the most weight to the studies with the most striking findings
rationale: Pooling increases the effective sample size and so tightens the confidence interval around the combined effect. It cannot fix bias built into the original studies, weights studies by precision rather than by how striking they are, and cannot extend findings to populations no study included.

stem: In a meta-analysis, heterogeneity refers to:
options: the use of different databases in the search
variation in the results across studies beyond what chance would explain
the total number of participants across all the studies
the difference in size between the very largest and the smallest study
rationale: Heterogeneity is genuine inconsistency among study effects, more than sampling variation alone would produce, which prompts caution about a single pooled figure. It is not the combined sample size, the spread of study sizes, or the choice of databases.

stem: When studies in a meta-analysis show substantial heterogeneity, a random-effects model is often preferred because it:
options: removes the differences between the studies from the result
leaves the smaller studies out of the analysis
produces a narrower confidence interval than a fixed-effect model
makes allowance for genuine variation in the true effect between studies
rationale: A random-effects model is suited to heterogeneity because it treats the true effect as varying across studies and reflects that in a wider, more honest interval. It does not narrow the interval, it cannot remove real differences, and it still includes the smaller studies.

stem: A random-effects meta-analysis differs from a fixed-effect one in that it assumes:
options: the largest study should dominate the pooled result
every study is estimating exactly the same single true effect
the studies were chosen at random from those available
the true effect may genuinely vary from one study to another
rationale: A random-effects model allows the underlying effect to differ across studies and reflects that extra variation in its estimate. Assuming one shared true effect is the fixed-effect model, the word random does not mean studies were randomly sampled, and neither model is defined by letting the largest study dominate.
