rationale: Specificity is the share of those who genuinely do not have the condition whom the test correctly clears as negative, so it measures correct exclusion among true non-cases. The share of those with the condition correctly called positive is sensitivity. The share of negative testers who truly lack the condition is the negative predictive value. The share of positive testers who truly have it is the positive predictive value.

stem: The probability that someone who tests positive genuinely has the condition is captured by a test's:
options: specificity
sensitivity
negative predictive value
positive predictive value
rationale: The probability that a positive result is a true case is the positive predictive value, which reads from the test result back to disease status. Sensitivity runs the other way, from those who truly have the condition to a positive result. Specificity concerns true non-cases and negative results. The negative predictive value concerns those who test negative, not positive.

stem: A false positive and a false negative differ in that:
options: both are correct results, one identifying a case and the other a non-case
a false negative is what lowers a test's specificity, while a false positive is what lowers its sensitivity
a false positive is a positive test in someone without the condition, while a false negative is a negative test in someone who has it
a false positive is a negative test in someone with the condition, while a false negative is a positive test in someone without it
rationale: A false positive is a positive test in a person who does not have the condition, and a false negative is a negative test in a person who does; these are the test's two kinds of error. Defining a false positive as a negative test in someone who has the condition, and a false negative as a positive test in someone without it, reverses the two. Calling both correct results misreads the word "false," which marks an error in each. And the links to the metrics run the other way: a false negative, a missed case, is what lowers sensitivity, while a false positive, a false alarm, is what lowers specificity.

stem: When the same test is used in a population where the condition is rarer, which of its measures changes?
options: the predictive values change, while sensitivity and specificity do not
none of the measures change, since they are fixed properties of the test
all four measures change in proportion to the prevalence
sensitivity and specificity change, while the predictive values stay the same
rationale: Predictive values depend on how common the condition is, so moving the test to a lower-prevalence population lowers the positive predictive value and raises the negative predictive value, while sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself and stay the same. Saying sensitivity and specificity change while predictive values hold reverses which measures are prevalence-dependent. Saying all four change treats sensitivity and specificity as prevalence-dependent, which they are not. Saying none change ignores that predictive values shift with prevalence.

stem: A clinician needs a first-line test for a serious condition where missing a true case would be dangerous, so no case should be overlooked. The most important property for this test is:
options: high positive predictive value
high negative predictive value
high sensitivity
high specificity
rationale: When missing a case is the danger, the test must catch nearly all true cases, so high sensitivity matters most, and a negative result from a sensitive test reliably rules the condition out. High specificity minimises false alarms, which suits ruling a condition in rather than ensuring none is missed. A high positive predictive value and a high negative predictive value are both desirable, but they depend on how common the condition is as well as on the test, so they are not properties the test can be built for directly, whereas sensitivity is intrinsic to the test.

stem: A screening programme is concerned that too many healthy people are being sent for invasive and costly follow-up after a positive screen. To reduce this, it should prioritise a test with:
options: high sensitivity, so that few people with the condition screen negative
a high negative predictive value, so that a negative screen is usually correct
high specificity, so that few people without the condition screen positive
a high false-positive rate, so that borderline cases are flagged for review
rationale: To cut the number of healthy people wrongly sent for follow-up, the programme needs few false positives, so it should prioritise high specificity, which correctly clears true non-cases. High sensitivity reduces missed cases but does nothing to limit false alarms among the healthy. A high negative predictive value concerns how far a negative screen can be trusted, not how many healthy people screen positive. A high false-positive rate would worsen the problem by flagging more healthy people, so seeking it is the opposite of what is needed.

stem: Raising the positivity threshold of a test, so that a stronger result is needed to call someone positive, will typically:
options: leave both sensitivity and specificity unchanged
increase both sensitivity and specificity
reduce specificity but increase sensitivity
increase specificity but reduce sensitivity
rationale: A higher threshold means fewer people are called positive, so more true non-cases are correctly cleared, raising specificity, but more true cases are missed, lowering sensitivity; the two move in opposite directions. Raising both at once cannot be done by moving the threshold, since it trades one for the other. Saying specificity falls while sensitivity rises reverses the effect of a stricter cut-off. And the threshold does affect both, so saying they are unchanged is wrong.

stem: In a screening programme, "uptake" refers to:
options: the proportion of the eligible population who actually take part in the screening
the proportion of those screened who are found to have the condition
the proportion of positive screens that are later confirmed as true cases
the proportion of those screened who go on to receive treatment
rationale: Uptake is the share of the eligible population who come forward and take part, so it measures participation and matters because low uptake limits a programme's reach and can skew who is covered. The share of those screened found to have the condition is the detection rate, or yield, a different measure. The share of positive screens later confirmed is the positive predictive value. The share going on to receive treatment is a downstream measure of the care pathway, not participation in screening.

stem: An age-standardised rate for a population represents:
options: the population's crude rate after its oldest and youngest age groups are set aside
the rate the population would have if its age structure matched a chosen standard
the average of the population's age-specific rates, giving each age group equal weight
the rate observed in the age group that contributes the most cases
rationale: A standardised rate is a hypothetical figure: it is the rate a population would show if its age structure matched an agreed standard, which is what lets different populations be compared fairly. It is not the crude rate with certain age groups set aside, since standardisation reweights every age group rather than dropping any. It is not an equal-weighted average of the age-specific rates, because the standard structure gives each age group its own weight. And it is not the rate in whichever age group contributes the most cases, since all age groups feed in, weighted by the standard.

stem: A crude rate for a whole population can mislead when two populations are compared because it:
options: counts only formally diagnosed cases, so milder cases are missed
is expressed per head of population, so a larger population will show a lower rate
reflects the population's age or other structure rather than the underlying risk
removes the effect of age, making the two populations look artificially similar
rationale: A crude rate lumps the whole population together, so it is shaped by the age or other structure of that population, and two populations with different structures can differ on the crude rate even at the same underlying risk. Being expressed per head does not mean a larger population shows a lower rate; a rate is a ratio and does not fall simply because the population is bigger. Missing milder, undiagnosed cases is an ascertainment problem that affects any rate, crude or standardised, so it is not what makes the crude rate specifically misleading across populations. And a crude rate does not remove the effect of age, which is precisely what standardisation, not the crude rate, does.

stem: After standardising the rates of two areas to the same population structure, a difference that remains between them is best interpreted as:
options: a difference in underlying risk, now that structure has been accounted for
an artefact of standardisation that should be disregarded
proof that conditions in the higher area are causing the difference
a difference still driven by the two areas' differing age structures
rationale: Standardisation removes the effect of differing population structures, so a difference that remains reflects a difference in underlying risk rather than composition. It does not by itself prove that conditions in the higher area cause the difference, since standardisation adjusts for structure, not for every other factor that might differ between the areas. It is not an artefact to disregard; the remaining difference is the meaningful signal standardisation exists to expose. And it is not still driven by differing age structures, since standardising to a common structure is exactly what removes that effect.

stem: An age-standardised rate adjusts for:
options: differences in the underlying risk of the condition between populations
differences in the total size of the populations being compared
differences in the accuracy of case recording between populations
differences in the age structure of the populations being compared
rationale: Age-standardisation removes the effect of differing age structures, so two populations can be compared without age composition driving the difference. It does not adjust for the total size of the populations, since rates already account for size through their denominators. It does not correct differences in how accurately cases are recorded, which is a data-quality matter. And it does not remove differences in underlying risk; those are exactly what a fair comparison is meant to reveal once age is accounted for.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes direct from indirect standardisation?
options: both apply the same standard rates to the same standard structure, and differ only in how the result is presented
direct applies standard rates to each population's own structure, while indirect applies each population's own age-specific rates to a standard structure
direct standardisation adjusts for differences in age, while indirect standardisation adjusts for differences in population size
direct applies each population's own age-specific rates to a standard structure, while indirect applies standard rates to each population's own structure
rationale: In direct standardisation each population's own age-specific rates are applied to one standard age structure, so the resulting rates differ only because of the rates; in indirect standardisation a standard set of rates is applied to each population's own structure, producing a ratio of observed to expected cases. The option that applies standard rates to each population's own structure while calling that the direct method swaps the two. Saying both apply the same rates to the same structure is wrong, since that would make them identical, which they are not. And indirect standardisation does not adjust for population size: both methods adjust for age structure, differing only in which component, the rates or the structure, is taken as the standard.

stem: Two regions have the same age-specific death rates, but region A has a much older population than region B. Comparing the two, you would expect that:
options: region B has the higher crude rate, because it has more younger people
the crude and age-standardised rates are equal in both regions
region A has the higher crude rate and also the higher age-standardised rate
region A has the higher crude rate, while their standardised rates are about equal
rationale: With identical age-specific rates, the two regions differ only in age structure, so region A's older population gives it more deaths per head overall and a higher crude rate, while standardising to a common structure makes their rates about equal, revealing the same underlying risk. Saying region A also has the higher standardised rate misses that the age-specific rates are identical, so standardisation equalises them. Saying region B has the higher crude rate reverses the effect of its younger population. Saying crude and standardised rates are equal in both ignores that age structure lifts region A's crude rate above its standardised one.

stem: Two areas' age-standardised rates can be compared directly only when:
options: the two areas had the same age structure to begin with
each has been standardised to its own most recent population
both have been standardised to the same standard population
the two areas have the same total population size
rationale: A directly standardised rate depends on the standard structure it was calculated against, so two such rates can be compared only if both used the same standard; otherwise a difference could come from the choice of standard rather than from the areas. Standardising each area to its own population reintroduces exactly the structural differences standardisation is meant to remove. Equal total population size is beside the point, since rates already account for size. And if the two areas had shared an age structure to begin with there would be nothing to standardise, so that is not the condition for comparing standardised rates.

stem: Crude and standardised rates suit different jobs. For which of these is a crude rate the more appropriate measure?
options: comparing two districts whose populations differ greatly in age
ranking all the districts in the country from highest to lowest risk
judging whether a single district's rate has truly risen over the past thirty years, as its population has aged
estimating how many cases a single district must resource this year, to plan its local services
rationale: A crude rate gives the actual number of cases relative to the real population, so it is the right basis for resourcing a single district's services here and now. Comparing two districts whose populations differ greatly in age needs a standardised rate, so that the age gap does not drive the comparison. Judging whether one district's rate has truly risen over thirty years also needs standardisation, since the population has aged over that time and a crude rise could reflect ageing rather than a real change in risk. And ranking all the districts by risk is a comparison across places with different age structures, which again calls for standardised rates.

stem: In the NHS, SNOMED CT is best described as:
options: a messaging standard used to move clinical data between separate systems
a diagnosis classification used to group conditions for national statistical returns and analysis
a procedure classification used to code operations and interventions
a structured clinical terminology used to record the detail of patient care in electronic records
rationale: SNOMED CT is a clinical terminology: a coded vocabulary for recording what happens in care at the point it is recorded. The diagnosis-grouping option describes ICD-10, whose job is statistical classification, not clinical recording. The procedure-coding option describes OPCS-4. The messaging option describes an interoperability standard such as HL7 FHIR, which moves data rather than defining clinical terms.

stem: Within NHS coded data, ICD-10 is used to:
options: define the secure route by which coded data is transferred between organisations
classify diagnoses and causes of illness or death into defined categories
record the fine detail of clinical findings during a consultation
code the specific surgical procedures a patient undergoes
rationale: ICD-10 is a classification of diagnoses and causes, used to group conditions consistently for analysis and returns. Recording fine clinical detail at the point of care is what SNOMED CT does. Coding procedures is the job of OPCS-4. Defining a secure transfer route describes a messaging mechanism such as MESH, not a classification.

stem: OPCS-4 is the NHS standard used to classify:
options: the property addresses used to link records across services
the full clinical narrative recorded during an episode of care
operative procedures and interventions carried out on patients
diagnoses and underlying causes of a patient's condition
rationale: OPCS-4 classifies procedures and interventions, the operative side of an episode. Classifying diagnoses and causes is ICD-10. Recording the full clinical narrative is SNOMED CT terminology. Property addresses for linkage describes the UPRN, which is an identifier, not a procedure classification.

stem: An analyst needs to record the precise clinical detail of each patient contact in the electronic record, and separately to produce grouped diagnosis counts for a national return. The two coding systems that fit these two tasks, in order, are:
options: SNOMED CT for recording the clinical detail, and ICD-10 for the grouped diagnosis counts
OPCS-4 for recording the clinical detail, and ICD-10 for the grouped diagnosis counts
ICD-10 for recording the clinical detail, and SNOMED CT for the grouped diagnosis counts
SNOMED CT for both tasks, since one terminology can serve recording and statistical grouping equally
rationale: SNOMED CT is built for recording detailed clinical care; ICD-10 is built for classifying diagnoses into groups for statistics, so the key pairs each system with the task it is designed for. Pairing ICD-10 with the clinical detail and SNOMED CT with the counts reverses the two. Using SNOMED CT for both tasks treats a recording terminology as if it were also a statistical classification, which is the distinction being tested. Substituting OPCS-4 for the recording role puts a procedure classification where the clinical recording terminology belongs.

stem: To count how many patients received a particular surgical operation in a year, the appropriate coded field to analyse is the one populated using:
options: SNOMED CT, because it records the free clinical narrative of the operation note
the NHS number, because it uniquely identifies each patient in the count
ICD-10, because it classifies the diagnoses that led to admission
OPCS-4, because it classifies the procedures and interventions performed
rationale: Counting operations means analysing procedure codes, which is exactly what OPCS-4 classifies. ICD-10 would count diagnoses, not procedures. SNOMED CT records clinical detail but is not the procedure classification used for this national count. The NHS number identifies patients but says nothing about which procedure was done.

stem: The agreed standard for recording structured clinical information in NHS electronic patient records is:
options: HL7 FHIR
SNOMED CT
OPCS-4
ICD-10
rationale: SNOMED CT is the standard for structured clinical content in the record itself. ICD-10 and OPCS-4 are classifications applied for analysis and reporting rather than the primary recording terminology. HL7 FHIR is an interoperability standard for exchanging data between systems, not for recording clinical content within a record.

stem: ICD-10 codes are central to national health statistics mainly because they:
options: record clinical observations at the level of detail used in day-to-day patient care
capture the full operative detail that is needed to audit surgical activity within a single provider
carry the secure addressing needed to route records between separate organisations
provide consistent diagnosis categories that allow conditions to be counted and compared across the system
rationale: ICD-10's value for statistics is a consistent, shared set of diagnosis categories, which makes counting and comparison possible. Full operative detail for surgical audit is OPCS-4 territory. Day-to-day clinical detail is SNOMED CT. Secure addressing for routing is a messaging function such as MESH, unrelated to diagnosis classification.

stem: Reviewing a coded hospital record, an analyst sees an entry for "excision of lesion" captured as an OPCS-4 code. This entry represents:
options: a procedure the patient underwent
the diagnosis that explained the patient's admission
a structured clinical finding recorded during assessment
the unique identifier linking this record to others
rationale: An OPCS-4 code records a procedure, so an excision coded in OPCS-4 is the operation performed. The diagnosis explaining admission would sit in ICD-10. A structured clinical finding would be SNOMED CT. A unique identifier linking records is the NHS number, not a procedure code.

stem: A feature that distinguishes SNOMED CT from a classification such as ICD-10 is that SNOMED CT:
options: assigns each case to a single mutually exclusive statistical category
specifies the secure transport route used to exchange records between separate systems
is a terminology of clinical concepts that can be combined to express detailed meaning
is limited to coding the procedures performed during an admission
rationale: SNOMED CT is concept-based and lets coded concepts be combined to express detail, which is what sets a terminology apart from a fixed classification. Assigning each case to one mutually exclusive category describes how a classification like ICD-10 works. Being limited to procedures describes OPCS-4. Specifying secure transport describes a messaging standard, not a terminology.

stem: The general difference between a clinical terminology and a statistical classification is that a terminology is designed to:
options: record what is clinically true about a patient in detail, while a classification groups cases into categories for analysis
uniquely identify individual patients across datasets, while a classification uniquely identifies the procedures done
group cases into broad categories for analysis, while a classification records the fine clinical detail of care
transport data securely between separate systems, while a classification stores that data locally in one place
rationale: A terminology records detailed clinical truth; a classification groups cases for analysis, so the key states the distinction the right way round. Casting the terminology as the grouper and the classification as the detailed recorder reverses the two roles. Framing the pair as transport versus local storage swaps in an interoperability idea, not the terminology-classification distinction. Framing it as identifying patients versus identifying procedures describes identifiers, not either of the two concepts in question.

stem: ICD-10 is organised so that individual diagnoses sit within broader groupings of related conditions. This arrangement mainly helps analysts to:
options: code the procedures carried out alongside each diagnosis
exchange the coded records securely with another organisation
aggregate related diagnoses to a broader level for counting and comparison
record extra clinical detail that a flat code list could not capture
rationale: A hierarchy of diagnoses lets analysts roll individual codes up to broader groups, which is what makes comparison and aggregation work. Capturing extra clinical detail is a strength of SNOMED CT, not the point of a diagnosis hierarchy. Coding procedures is OPCS-4. Exchanging records securely is a messaging function, unrelated to how a classification is structured.

stem: Data recorded in SNOMED CT sometimes has to be mapped to ICD-10 before it is used in national statistics. The main reason is that:
options: ICD-10 records more clinical detail than SNOMED CT and so replaces it for detailed analysis
mapping is the secure mechanism by which coded records are transferred between separate organisations for sharing
detailed clinical terms need translating into the broader diagnosis categories that national returns are built on
SNOMED CT cannot be stored in an electronic record at all without an equivalent ICD-10 code
rationale: National returns are built on ICD-10 categories, so detailed SNOMED CT terms are mapped across to fit them, which is a translation between a terminology and a classification. The claim that SNOMED CT cannot be stored without an ICD-10 equivalent is untrue, since it is stored directly in records. The claim that ICD-10 holds more detail and so replaces SNOMED CT inverts the relationship, since ICD-10 holds less detail, not more. Treating mapping as a secure transfer mechanism confuses a translation of meaning with the movement of data.

stem: A public health team wants to compare rates of a particular diagnosis between two regions using routine hospital data. The coded field they should base the comparison on is the one populated with:
options: OPCS-4 procedure codes
ICD-10 diagnosis codes
NHS numbers for the patients involved
SNOMED CT operation-note terms
rationale: Comparing diagnosis rates means analysing diagnosis codes, which ICD-10 provides in a consistent, comparable form. OPCS-4 would tell them about procedures, not diagnoses. SNOMED CT operation-note terms describe care in detail but are not the classification used for this comparison. NHS numbers identify patients but carry no information about the diagnosis being compared.

stem: Among the coding systems used in the NHS, the one specifically intended for interventions and operations is:
options: ICD-10
SNOMED CT
MESH
OPCS-4
rationale: OPCS-4 is the classification for procedures and interventions. ICD-10 classifies diagnoses. SNOMED CT is the clinical recording terminology. MESH is a message transport mechanism for moving data, not a coding system at all.

stem: A DCB-mandated information standard in health and care is best understood as:
options: a security tool that scores an organisation's data protection arrangements each year
a formally mandated standard that sets how specified data must be defined or handled
a voluntary guideline that organisations may adopt at their discretion
a messaging format used to exchange records between systems
rationale: A DCB-mandated standard is a formally required rule about how data is defined or handled, carrying an obligation to comply. A voluntary, discretionary guideline is the opposite of a mandated standard. An annual data-protection scoring tool describes the DSPT. A messaging format for exchange describes an interoperability standard, not a governance standard.

stem: The role of the Data Coordination Board (DCB) in NHS information standards is to:
options: host the national services through which records are shared
mandate the information standards that organisations are required to follow
carry out the annual data security self-assessment for each organisation
assign the unique patient identifier used to link records
rationale: The DCB's role is to mandate information standards, giving them their required status. The annual data security self-assessment is the DSPT. Assigning the unique patient identifier describes the NHS number. Hosting national sharing services describes the NHS Spine.

stem: An Information Standards Notice (ISN) issued by NHS England functions to:
options: publish an information standard and set out what organisations must do to comply
provide the secure transport used to move data between separate organisations
record the detailed clinical terms used in a patient's care
assess an organisation's compliance with data security requirements
rationale: An ISN is the notice that publishes an information standard and states the compliance obligations attached to it. Secure transport between organisations is a messaging function such as MESH. Recording detailed clinical terms is SNOMED CT. Assessing data security compliance is the DSPT.

stem: A new requirement for how a dataset must be recorded is being made compulsory across NHS organisations. The instrument through which this requirement is formally published and mandated is:
options: an Information Standards Notice
the Data Security and Protection Toolkit
an application programming interface
the NHS Data Dictionary
rationale: An Information Standards Notice is the route by which a standard is formally published and made compulsory. The Data Security and Protection Toolkit assures data security but does not publish data standards. The NHS Data Dictionary defines data items but is not the mechanism that mandates a new requirement. An application programming interface is a means of exchanging data, not of mandating a standard.

stem: The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is used by NHS and social care organisations to:
options: mandate new information standards for organisations right across the wider system
exchange structured clinical data with other organisations that need it
classify the diagnoses recorded in their patients' records into categories
assess and demonstrate that they meet required data security and protection standards
rationale: The DSPT is the tool through which an organisation assesses and evidences that it meets data security and protection standards. Classifying diagnoses is ICD-10. Exchanging structured clinical data is an interoperability function such as HL7 FHIR. Mandating new information standards is the role of the DCB, not an assurance toolkit.

stem: A distinctive feature of the DSPT is that organisations use it to:
options: look up the agreed definition of each data item that they collect and record in the record
complete a periodic self-assessment against a set of data security and protection standards
receive a formal notice that a new data standard has now become mandatory
transmit patient records securely to another care provider when needed
rationale: The DSPT is completed as a periodic self-assessment against defined data security standards. Looking up agreed data item definitions is what the NHS Data Dictionary is for. Receiving formal notice of a newly mandatory standard describes an ISN. Transmitting records securely to another provider describes a messaging mechanism such as MESH.

stem: The difference between the DSPT and an information standard is that the DSPT is concerned with:
options: how records move between systems, while an information standard governs who may access them
how data items are named, while an information standard governs how securely they are stored
how securely data is handled, while an information standard governs how the data itself is defined
which patient a record belongs to, while an information standard governs how records are exchanged
rationale: The DSPT is about the security of data handling, whereas an information standard sets how the data is defined and structured, so the key separates the two by their true concerns. Casting the DSPT as concerned with naming items and the standard with secure storage reverses them, putting definition on the wrong side. Casting the pair as patient identity versus record exchange swaps in the NHS number and messaging, not either concept here. Casting it as how records move versus who may access them swaps in transport and access control, again neither of the two concepts in question.

stem: An information standard in the NHS is mainly concerned with specifying:
options: how well an organisation protects and safeguards the data that it holds
how a particular set of data must be defined, structured or recorded
which national services are used to share records
the unique number that identifies each patient
rationale: An information standard specifies how data must be defined, structured or recorded, giving consistency across organisations. How well data is protected is the DSPT's concern. The national services used to share records describe the NHS Spine. The unique patient number is the NHS number.

stem: An organisation finds that a dataset it submits is covered by a DCB-mandated information standard. The practical consequence is that the organisation:
options: is required to record and submit that data in the way the standard specifies
must obtain a unique identifier for the dataset before it can be shared
may choose whether to adopt the standard depending on local priorities
must complete a security self-assessment before submitting the data
rationale: A mandated standard carries an obligation, so the organisation must record and submit the data as specified. Treating adoption as optional contradicts the meaning of mandated. Completing a security self-assessment is the DSPT, a separate requirement not triggered by the standard itself. Obtaining a unique identifier before sharing conflates the situation with an identifier or linkage step that the standard does not impose.

stem: Governance standards for patient confidential data exist mainly to:
options: classify diagnoses so that conditions can be counted nationally
define the clinical terms used to record a patient's care
provide the interface through which systems query each other's data directly
set out how sensitive data must be protected and handled safely across the system
rationale: Governance standards set the rules for protecting and safely handling sensitive data. Defining clinical terms is SNOMED CT. Classifying diagnoses for national counts is ICD-10. Providing a query interface between systems is an API.

stem: When a new information standard becomes mandatory, the Information Standards Notice serves as the:
options: register of agreed definitions for each data item in use
formal publication that sets out the standard and its compliance requirements
annual return through which an organisation's security compliance is demonstrated
secure channel used to transmit the affected records
rationale: The ISN is the formal publication of a standard and its compliance requirements. The annual return demonstrating security compliance is the DSPT. The register of agreed data item definitions is the NHS Data Dictionary. The secure transmission channel is a messaging mechanism such as MESH.

stem: Among the following, the instrument used to give assurance about data security and protection is the:
options: NHS Data Dictionary
Data Security and Protection Toolkit
Information Standards Notice
Data Coordination Board
rationale: The Data Security and Protection Toolkit is the assurance instrument for data security. The Information Standards Notice publishes standards rather than assuring security. The NHS Data Dictionary defines data items. The Data Coordination Board mandates standards.

stem: HL7 FHIR is best described as:
options: a classification for grouping diagnoses into categories in national statistical returns
a terminology for recording the clinical detail of a patient's care
a toolkit through which an organisation assesses its own data security
a standard for exchanging health data between different systems in a structured form
rationale: HL7 FHIR is an interoperability standard for exchanging health data between systems in a structured form. Recording clinical detail is SNOMED CT. Assessing data security is the DSPT. Grouping diagnoses for statistics is ICD-10.

stem: A conceptual feature of HL7 FHIR is that it represents health information as:
options: a single secure mailbox for transferring files between organisations
mutually exclusive diagnosis categories for statistical grouping
modular resources that systems can exchange and combine in a consistent way
a self-assessment of an organisation's data protection arrangements
rationale: FHIR represents information as modular resources that can be exchanged and combined consistently, which is what supports interoperability. Mutually exclusive diagnosis categories describe a classification like ICD-10. A secure mailbox for file transfer describes MESH. A data protection self-assessment describes the DSPT.

stem: In the exchange of health data, an application programming interface (API) provides:
options: a mandated rule for how a dataset must be defined
a defined way for one system to request and receive data from another
an annual assessment of how securely data is protected
a coded vocabulary for recording clinical findings in the record
rationale: An API gives systems a defined way to request and receive data from one another. A coded vocabulary for clinical findings is SNOMED CT. An annual security assessment is the DSPT. A mandated rule for defining a dataset is an information standard.

stem: Message Exchange for Social Care and Health (MESH) is used to:
options: define the agreed meaning of each data item collected
classify the procedures a patient has undergone
transfer data securely between health and care organisations
record structured clinical concepts at the point of care
rationale: MESH is a secure mechanism for transferring data between health and care organisations. Defining the agreed meaning of data items is the NHS Data Dictionary. Classifying procedures is OPCS-4. Recording structured clinical concepts is SNOMED CT.

stem: Two systems need to agree both on the format of the clinical data they share and on a secure route to move it between organisations. The pairing that fits these two needs, in order, is:
options: an API for the format of the data, and HL7 FHIR for the secure route
HL7 FHIR for the format of the data, and MESH for the secure route
HL7 FHIR for both the format and the secure route
MESH for the format of the data, and HL7 FHIR for the secure route
rationale: HL7 FHIR is a standard for how the data is structured, and MESH is a mechanism for moving it securely, so the key pairs each with the need it serves. Pairing MESH with the format and FHIR with the route reverses the two. Using FHIR for both the format and the route gives one standard both jobs, ignoring that FHIR does not provide the secure transport itself. Using an API for the format and FHIR for the route miscasts an API as a data format and FHIR as a transport, swapping both roles.

stem: A service needs to look up a single patient's current record from another system at the moment of care. The most suitable form of access is:
options: a periodic national submission of the dataset
a scheduled bulk extract of all records sent overnight
a secure mailbox transfer of a batch file
an API that returns the specific record on request
rationale: An API returns a specific record on demand, which suits a real-time single-patient lookup. A scheduled overnight bulk extract delivers everything in batch, too late and too broad for a point-of-care query. A periodic national submission serves central collection, not live lookup. A secure mailbox batch transfer, such as MESH, moves files in bulk rather than answering a live query.

stem: In health and care data, interoperability refers to the ability of:
options: different systems to exchange data and use it in a consistent, meaningful way
a single system to store large volumes of data efficiently in one place
an organisation to demonstrate that it protects its data securely
an analyst to classify diagnoses into comparable statistical categories
rationale: Interoperability is about different systems exchanging data and being able to use it meaningfully. Efficient large-volume storage in one system describes data warehousing, not interoperability. Demonstrating secure protection is the DSPT. Classifying diagnoses into comparable categories is ICD-10.

stem: Among the following, the one that provides a secure transport route for messages between health and care organisations is:
options: the NHS Data Dictionary
MESH
SNOMED CT
HL7 FHIR
rationale: MESH provides the secure transport route for messages between organisations. HL7 FHIR standardises the structure of the data being exchanged rather than transporting it. SNOMED CT is the clinical recording terminology. The NHS Data Dictionary defines data items.

stem: A developer wants records shared between two systems to arrive as defined, structured elements that the receiving system can interpret without manual reformatting. The standard that supports this is:
options: HL7 FHIR
MESH
the DSPT
OPCS-4
rationale: HL7 FHIR defines structured elements that a receiving system can interpret directly, which is what the developer needs. MESH would move the data securely but does not define its structure. The DSPT assures data security and has no role in structuring exchanged data. OPCS-4 is a procedure classification, unrelated to exchange.

stem: Compared with a person manually exporting and emailing a data file, API-based access mainly offers:
options: a stronger legal obligation to record the data in the mandated way
an assessment of how securely the data is being protected by the organisation
a repeatable, defined route for systems to request data directly from one another
an agreed dictionary of definitions for each data item that is exchanged
rationale: An API gives a repeatable, defined route for systems to exchange data directly, unlike an ad hoc manual export. A legal obligation to record data in a mandated way is an information standard. An agreed dictionary of definitions is the NHS Data Dictionary. An assessment of data protection is the DSPT.

stem: Describing exchanged data as "structured" rather than free text mainly means that the data:
options: has been given a unique identifier for each patient
is organised into defined fields that a receiving system can process consistently
has been checked against an organisation's own data security standards before release
has been classified into national diagnosis categories
rationale: Structured data is organised into defined fields a receiving system can process consistently, which is the point of structuring it for exchange. Checking against security standards is the DSPT. Classifying into diagnosis categories is ICD-10. Giving each patient a unique identifier is the NHS number.

stem: The named standard whose purpose is to make structured clinical data exchangeable between systems is:
options: the DSPT
the NHS number
ICD-10
HL7 FHIR
rationale: HL7 FHIR is the standard for exchanging structured clinical data between systems. ICD-10 classifies diagnoses for statistics. The DSPT assures data security. The NHS number is a patient identifier.

stem: The NHS Data Dictionary is best described as:
options: a toolkit through which an organisation assesses its own data security
a secure mechanism for transferring records between separate organisations
a classification of diagnoses used to group conditions consistently in national statistics
a reference that sets out the agreed definitions of data items and terms used across the NHS
rationale: The NHS Data Dictionary is the reference for agreed definitions of data items and terms, supporting consistency across the NHS. A secure transfer mechanism is MESH. A diagnosis classification is ICD-10. A data security assessment toolkit is the DSPT.

stem: Alongside the Data Dictionary, the NHS Data Model is mainly concerned with:
options: how securely the data is transferred between two separate organisations
which diagnoses should be grouped together for national statistical counting and returns
how the defined data items relate to one another within the wider structure of the data
how an organisation evidences its data protection arrangements each year
rationale: The NHS Data Model describes how defined data items relate to one another, the structure that sits alongside the dictionary's definitions. Secure transfer between organisations is MESH. Grouping diagnoses for national counting is ICD-10. Evidencing data protection annually is the DSPT.

stem: The main value of the NHS Data Dictionary for analysts working across different organisations is that it:
options: scores how well each organisation protects the sensitive data it holds
moves data securely from one organisation to another whenever records are shared between them
gives everyone the same agreed meaning for each data item, so data can be compared reliably
assigns a unique identifier to each patient recorded in the dataset
rationale: The Data Dictionary supplies a shared, agreed meaning for each data item, which is what lets data be compared reliably across organisations. Moving data securely is MESH. Assigning a unique patient identifier is the NHS number. Scoring data protection is the DSPT.

stem: The NHS Spine is best described as:
options: a reference listing the agreed definition of each data item used in records across the whole NHS
a classification used to group diagnoses for national statistical returns
an annual assessment of how well an organisation protects its data
the national infrastructure that supports key services and the sharing of information across the NHS
rationale: The NHS Spine is the national infrastructure supporting core services and information sharing across the NHS. A classification grouping diagnoses is ICD-10. A reference of agreed data item definitions is the NHS Data Dictionary. An annual data security assessment is the DSPT.

stem: The NHS number is best described as:
options: a unique identifier assigned to a patient across the health and care system
a secure route for transferring a patient's record to another provider
a code that classifies the patient's diagnosis into a category
a reference that defines each data item recorded in a patient record
rationale: The NHS number is a unique identifier for a patient across the system. A code classifying a diagnosis is ICD-10. A reference defining data items is the NHS Data Dictionary. A secure transfer route is MESH.

stem: An analyst wants to bring together a patient's hospital records and community records into a single linked view. The identifier that makes this linkage possible is the:
options: ICD-10 code, which records the patient's diagnosis in each dataset
NHS number, which identifies the same patient across both datasets
OPCS-4 code, which records any procedures in each dataset
UPRN, which identifies the property associated with the patient
rationale: The NHS number identifies the same patient in both datasets, which is what enables their records to be linked. An ICD-10 code records a diagnosis but does not identify the individual across datasets. An OPCS-4 code records procedures, not identity. The UPRN identifies a property, not a person, so it links on place rather than patient.

stem: The Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN) is used to:
options: identify a specific property or address consistently across datasets
define the agreed meaning of each data item collected
classify the procedures carried out during an admission
identify an individual patient across health and care records
rationale: The UPRN is a consistent identifier for a property or address across datasets. Identifying an individual patient is the NHS number. Classifying procedures is OPCS-4. Defining agreed data item meanings is the NHS Data Dictionary.

stem: A study needs to link records by household rather than by individual patient. The identifier suited to this is the:
options: UPRN, because it identifies the property the records share
SNOMED CT concept, because it records the clinical detail in each record
ICD-10 code, because it records the diagnoses in each record
NHS number, because it identifies each individual in the household
rationale: Linking by household means linking on the shared property, which is what the UPRN identifies. The NHS number identifies individuals, so it would link by person, not household. An ICD-10 code records diagnoses and does not identify a household. A SNOMED CT concept records clinical detail and carries no linkage role.

stem: In record linkage, a linkage key is best described as:
options: a common identifier that lets records about the same subject be joined across datasets
a secure channel through which records are transmitted between systems
a definition of the fields that each record is required to contain
a classification that groups records together by diagnosis for later statistical analysis
rationale: A linkage key is a common identifier that lets records about the same subject be joined across datasets. A classification grouping records by diagnosis is ICD-10. A secure transmission channel is MESH. A definition of required fields is an information standard or the Data Dictionary.

stem: A reason the NHS Spine matters for data flows is that it:
options: assesses how securely each organisation handles the data that it holds
defines the agreed meaning of each data item used in records across the NHS
classifies the diagnoses recorded during an episode of care into their set categories for counting
underpins national services that let organisations share and look up information about the same patient
rationale: The NHS Spine underpins national services that support sharing and looking up patient information across organisations. Defining agreed data item meanings is the NHS Data Dictionary. Classifying diagnoses is ICD-10. Assessing data security is the DSPT.

stem: The difference between the NHS Data Dictionary and the NHS Data Model is that the dictionary:
options: moves data between systems, while the model stores it securely
sets out how items relate, while the model sets out what each item means
sets out what each data item means, while the model sets out how the items relate to one another
identifies patients uniquely across datasets, while the model classifies their recorded diagnoses
rationale: The dictionary defines what each data item means and the model describes how items relate, so the key states the distinction the right way round. Casting the dictionary as describing relationships and the model as defining meanings reverses the two. Casting the pair as moving data versus storing it securely swaps in interoperability and warehousing ideas, not either concept here. Casting it as identifying patients versus classifying diagnoses swaps in identification and classification, again neither of the two concepts in question.

stem: A Patient Administration System (PAS) is best described as:
options: a local operational system that manages patient administration within a provider
a secure environment in which researchers analyse linked data in place without removing it
a classification used to group diagnoses for national statistics
a national collection into which providers submit their activity data
rationale: A PAS is a local operational system that manages patient administration within a provider, and is one of the sources feeding national data flows. A national collection receiving submitted data is the destination of a flow, such as SDCS Cloud, not the local source. A secure environment for analysing data in place is a TRE or SDE. A diagnosis classification is ICD-10.

stem: An Electronic Patient Record (EPR) system functions as:
options: a secure toolkit for assessing an organisation's data protection
a classification used to code the procedures a patient receives
a local system that holds the record of a patient's care within a provider
a national platform that links data from many providers for research
rationale: An EPR is a local system holding a patient's care record within a provider, and is one of the operational sources feeding national flows. A national platform linking many providers' data for research describes a federated platform or research environment, not a local source. A classification for coding procedures is OPCS-4. A data protection assessment toolkit is the DSPT.

stem: A provider's activity data begins in its operational systems and ends up in a national dataset available for secondary analysis. The direction of this data flow is:
options: between two local systems within the same provider
from a research environment back into the patient's record
from local operational systems into a national collection
from a national collection out to local operational systems
rationale: The flow runs from local operational systems up into a national collection, which is the standard direction for secondary-use data. The reverse, from national collection down to local systems, inverts the flow. A transfer between two local systems in one provider is not a national flow at all. A movement from a research environment back into the record misdescribes both ends.

stem: In NHS data flows, SDCS Cloud is best understood as:
options: a local system in which patient administration is managed
a terminology for recording clinical detail in the record
an identifier used to link a patient's records together across different datasets
a mechanism through which providers submit data into a national collection
rationale: SDCS Cloud is a mechanism through which providers submit data into a national collection, sitting at the collection end of a flow. A local system managing patient administration is a PAS. A terminology for recording clinical detail is SNOMED CT. An identifier linking records across datasets is the NHS number.

stem: Describing national data collection as running on a submission cycle mainly means that:
options: providers send their data to the national collection at defined, repeating intervals
data may be analysed only from within a secure research environment
data is corrected automatically each time one of its records is opened for viewing
each record is given a unique identifier at the moment it is created
rationale: A submission cycle means providers send data to the national collection at defined, repeating intervals. Automatic correction on opening a record is not what a submission cycle describes. Assigning a unique identifier at creation is an identifier function, not a cycle. Restricting analysis to a secure environment describes a TRE or SDE, a different concept.

stem: After data is collected nationally, it typically passes through validation and publication. These stages mainly serve to:
options: move the data securely from the provider to the national collection point
check the data for quality and then make the agreed outputs available for use
define the meaning of each data item before it is recorded
assign each patient a unique identifier within the dataset
rationale: Validation checks the collected data for quality, and publication makes the agreed outputs available, so the key describes both stages correctly. Moving data securely to the collection is the transport step that precedes collection, not validation or publication. Defining data item meanings is the Data Dictionary, done before recording. Assigning a unique identifier is the NHS number's role.

stem: In a federated data model, the defining idea is that:
options: all data is copied into a single central store before any of it can be analysed
data can be analysed only after it has been published nationally for use
data stays in its original locations and is queried in place rather than being pooled centrally
data is exchanged between systems using a shared messaging standard agreed by both parties
rationale: A federated model leaves data in its original locations and queries it in place, avoiding a central pool. Copying everything into a single central store describes a data warehouse, the opposite approach. Restricting analysis to after national publication misdescribes the model. Exchanging data using a shared messaging standard is interoperability, a different concept.

stem: The Federated Data Platform (FDP) is best described as:
options: a platform that lets organisations bring together and work with data while it remains federated
a toolkit through which an organisation assesses its own data security arrangements each year
a classification used to group diagnoses for national statistical returns
a terminology for recording the clinical detail of a patient's care
rationale: The FDP is a platform that lets organisations bring together and work with data on a federated basis. A classification grouping diagnoses is ICD-10. An annual data security assessment toolkit is the DSPT. A terminology for recording clinical detail is SNOMED CT.

stem: Researchers are given access to sensitive linked data on condition that they analyse it inside a controlled environment and do not take the raw data away. This arrangement describes a:
options: data warehouse that stores all records in a single central location
national submission cycle for routine data collection
messaging mechanism for transferring records between organisations
Trusted Research Environment or Secure Data Environment
rationale: Analysing sensitive data inside a controlled environment without removing the raw data is the defining feature of a Trusted Research Environment or Secure Data Environment. A national submission cycle concerns routine collection, not controlled analysis. A data warehouse is a central store, which does not by itself impose analyse-in-place access. A messaging mechanism transfers records rather than hosting analysis.

stem: A data warehouse differs from a federated model in that a warehouse:
options: identifies patients uniquely, whereas a federated model classifies their diagnoses
leaves data in place, whereas a federated model brings it into a central store
brings data together into a central store, whereas a federated model leaves it in place
transmits data securely, whereas a federated model defines how it is recorded
rationale: A warehouse brings data into a central store while a federated model leaves it in place, so the key states the contrast the right way round. Casting the warehouse as leaving data in place and the federated model as centralising it reverses the two. Casting the pair as secure transmission versus how data is recorded swaps in messaging and dictionary ideas, not either concept here. Casting it as identifying patients versus classifying diagnoses swaps in identification and classification, again neither of the two concepts in question.

stem: Among the following, the concept defined by analysing data in a secure setting without releasing the raw data is the:
options: submission cycle
data warehouse
application programming interface
Secure Data Environment
rationale: A Secure Data Environment is defined by analysing data in a controlled setting without releasing the raw data. A data warehouse is a central store and does not by itself define analyse-in-place access. A submission cycle concerns the timing of routine data collection. An application programming interface is a route for exchanging data between systems.

stem: In a data pipeline, the term raw data is best understood as data that has:
options: been published as a final output with accompanying metadata and methodology
been ingested in its original form, before cleaning or transformation
been organised, documented and shaped into a form ready for a specific analysis
had obvious errors corrected and inconsistent formats standardised, but is not yet shaped for analysis
rationale: Raw data is the source material as first received, with no cleaning or transformation. Data that has had errors corrected and formats standardised is cleaned data, a later stage. Data shaped and documented for a specific analysis is curated or analysis-ready data. A published output with metadata sits at the dissemination end, not at ingestion.

stem: The stage described as curated or analysis-ready data differs from cleaned data chiefly in that it has additionally been:
options: received from the source system without any processing applied
organised and documented into a form fit for a particular analytical purpose
encrypted and placed behind role-based access controls for security
stripped of duplicate rows and corrected for obvious data-entry errors
rationale: Curated or analysis-ready data goes beyond cleaning by being shaped and documented for a specific analytical purpose. Removing duplicates and correcting entry errors is the cleaning step that precedes it. Data received without processing is raw data. Encryption and access control are security properties of a store, not a processing stage.

stem: Describing data movement as a pipeline is mainly a way of expressing that:
options: data moves through a defined sequence of stages from source towards use
data is held in a single store that several teams can query directly
every analysis must be rebuilt by hand each time it is needed
data is exchanged between two organisations under a sharing agreement
rationale: A pipeline is the idea of data passing through a defined sequence of stages on its way from source to use. A single shared store that teams query is a storage arrangement, not a pipeline. Rebuilding analyses by hand is the opposite of a pipeline's automation. Exchange between organisations under an agreement is a data-sharing concept, not a pipeline.

stem: A batch refresh is best characterised by the fact that data is:
options: collected and processed in grouped sets on a schedule rather than continuously
made available only through a secure research environment to approved analysts
held permanently unchanged once it has first been loaded into the store
processed item by item as each new record arrives, with minimal delay
rationale: A batch refresh groups records and processes them on a schedule. Processing each record as it arrives with minimal delay describes streaming, the alternative cadence. Data held unchanged after first load describes an immutable store, not a refresh pattern. Availability only through a secure environment is an access-control property, unrelated to cadence.

stem: Streaming is most useful, compared with batch processing, when the priority is:
options: acting on each new record with as little delay as possible
reprocessing the entire dataset together at a fixed time each day
keeping the long-term archive of historical records unchanged
restricting who may query the data through assigned access roles
rationale: Streaming suits situations where low delay on each new record matters most. Reprocessing the whole dataset at a fixed time is batch processing, the opposite cadence. Keeping a historical archive unchanged is a retention concern. Restricting who may query the data is access control, not a cadence choice.

stem: A surveillance team receives a nightly file containing all of the previous day's laboratory results in one transfer. This arrangement is an example of:
options: a streaming feed, because results are delivered to the team as a continuous flow
an object store, because the file is held as a single unstructured blob
a batch refresh, because records are grouped and delivered on a fixed schedule
a curated dataset, because the results have been shaped for a specific analysis
rationale: Grouping a day's records into one scheduled nightly transfer is a batch refresh. A streaming feed would deliver each result continuously as it arose, not once a night. Whether the data has been shaped for analysis is a processing-stage question, separate from the delivery cadence. How the file is stored is a storage-model question, not a cadence.

stem: An analyst notes that a dataset has had inconsistent date formats standardised and impossible values removed, but has not yet been joined or documented for any particular study. This dataset is best described as being at the:
options: dissemination stage, since it is ready to be published as a statistical output
cleaned stage, with standardisation done but no shaping for a specific analysis
raw stage, since no processing of any kind has yet been applied to it
curated stage, since it has been documented and shaped for a defined analysis
rationale: Standardising formats and removing impossible values is the cleaning stage. Raw data would have had no processing at all, which is not the case here. Curated data would additionally be joined, documented and shaped for a specific analysis, which has not happened. Dissemination concerns published outputs, which is further downstream again.

stem: Within a processing pipeline, the main reason to keep the raw, cleaned and curated forms as distinct stages is that it:
options: removes the need to apply any access controls to the underlying data
means the data no longer needs to be exchanged between separate systems
guarantees that the published outputs will require no documented methodology
lets each transformation be traced and rerun without losing the original source
rationale: Keeping the stages distinct lets each transformation be traced and rerun while the original source is preserved. It does not remove the need for access controls, which apply regardless. It says nothing about whether outputs need documented methodology, which they still do. And it has no bearing on whether systems need to exchange data.

stem: Describing a refresh as continuous rather than scheduled is, in pipeline terms, a statement about the system's:
options: delivery cadence, meaning how often new data becomes available
provenance, meaning the traceability of data back to its source
access method, meaning how a consumer retrieves the data
storage model, meaning the type of store the data is held in
rationale: Whether a refresh is continuous or scheduled is a statement about delivery cadence. The type of store the data sits in is the storage model, a separate property. How a consumer retrieves the data is the access method. Traceability back to source is provenance, which is unaffected by how often data refreshes.

stem: When data is said to be analysis-ready, the readiness being claimed is principally that the data has been:
options: transferred to a second organisation under an agreed sharing arrangement
assigned a retention period after which it will be securely deleted
shaped and documented so a specific intended analysis can be run on it
received directly from the source with its original structure intact
rationale: Analysis-ready means the data has been shaped and documented for the intended analysis. Data with its original source structure intact is raw data. Transfer to another organisation under agreement is data sharing, not readiness. Assigning a retention period is a governance property and does not make data analysis-ready.

stem: A data warehouse is best described as a store designed to hold:
options: large unstructured files such as images and documents as discrete objects
structured, integrated data organised to support analysis across sources
the current operational records of a single application for day-to-day transactions
raw data of many kinds in its native form, structured or otherwise, kept for later use
rationale: A data warehouse holds structured, integrated data arranged for analysis across sources. A store that keeps raw data of many kinds in native form is a data lake. A store for large unstructured files as discrete objects is blob or object storage. A store of current operational records for one application is a transactional database.

stem: A data lake is distinguished from a data warehouse mainly by the fact that it:
options: holds only data that has been cleaned and curated before it is allowed in
holds structured records in tables linked by keys for a single application's use
holds data of varied kinds in its native form, without requiring a fixed structure first
holds structured data that has already been integrated and modelled for analysis
rationale: A data lake takes data of varied kinds in native form without imposing structure up front. Holding structured, modelled, integrated data is the warehouse it is contrasted with. Holding tables linked by keys for one application is a relational database. Requiring data to be cleaned and curated before entry is the opposite of a lake, which accepts raw data and defers structure.

stem: Blob or object storage is the storage model most suited to holding:
options: the day-to-day operational transactions of a single live application
large unstructured items such as images and documents, kept as whole objects
integrated structured data modelled specifically for cross-source analysis
rows and columns of structured records linked to one another by their keys
rationale: Blob or object storage suits large unstructured items kept as self-contained objects. Rows and columns linked by keys describe a relational database. Integrated structured data modelled for analysis is a warehouse. Day-to-day operational transactions of one application are held in a transactional database.

stem: A relational or transactional database is the appropriate storage model when the main need is to:
options: record and update structured operational data reliably as transactions occur
integrate data from many sources into a single model for analytical querying
keep unstructured media files as discrete objects for later retrieval
store large volumes of mixed raw data without deciding its structure beforehand
rationale: A relational or transactional database suits reliable recording and updating of structured operational data as transactions happen. Storing mixed raw data without a predetermined structure is a data lake. Keeping unstructured media as discrete objects is object storage. Integrating many sources into one analytical model is a data warehouse.

stem: In a relational database, a key is best understood as a column or set of columns used to:
options: store large binary files such as images alongside the structured records
define which users are permitted to read or write the table's contents
record the schedule on which the table is refreshed from its source
identify rows uniquely and to relate rows in one table to rows in another
rationale: A key identifies rows uniquely and relates rows across tables. Storing large binary files is the role of object storage, not a key. The refresh schedule is a cadence property held outside the table structure. Defining who may read or write is access control, governed separately from keys.

stem: A join in a relational database is the operation that:
options: stacks the rows of one table onto another that has the same columns
appends two text values end to end to form a single longer value
combines rows from two tables by matching them on a related column
splits one wide table into several narrower related tables
rationale: A join combines rows from two tables by matching on a related column. Stacking rows from a same-shaped table is a union, which adds rows rather than relating them. Appending two text values end to end is concatenation, an operation on values not tables. Splitting one wide table into narrower related ones is decomposition during normalisation, not a join.

stem: A normalised relational structure is one in which data is organised so that:
options: records are held as unstructured objects rather than rows and columns
all the fields a report needs are gathered into a single wide table
each fact is stored once across related tables, reducing duplication
data is grouped and delivered to consumers on a fixed schedule
rationale: A normalised structure stores each fact once across related tables to reduce duplication. Gathering all the fields a report needs into one wide table describes a flattened or analytical structure. Holding records as unstructured objects is object storage. Delivering data on a fixed schedule is a cadence, not a structural choice.

stem: A flattened or analytical table is often preferred over a normalised structure for analysis because it:
options: stores each fact only once across many related tables, which reduces duplication
brings the fields together into one table, so analytical querying is simpler
keeps data as discrete unstructured objects that are retrieved by name
limits access to the data to a defined set of approved analyst roles
rationale: A flattened table gathers the needed fields into one place, making analytical querying simpler. Storing each fact once across many tables is the normalised structure it is contrasted with. Keeping data as discrete unstructured objects is object storage. Limiting access to approved roles is access control, unrelated to table shape.

stem: SQL is best recognised as:
options: the standard language used to query and manipulate data held in structured tables
a storage model used for keeping large unstructured files as discrete named objects
a framework for mapping one coding scheme onto another between systems
a method of transferring grouped records to consumers on a fixed schedule
rationale: SQL is the standard language for querying and manipulating data in structured tables. A model for keeping unstructured files as objects is object storage. Transferring grouped records on a schedule is a batch cadence. Mapping one coding scheme onto another is an interoperability activity, not a query language.

stem: Retrieving data through an API rather than a provided extract chiefly means the consumer:
options: receives a fixed file of data prepared and sent to them by the provider
requests data programmatically from the system through a defined interface
works with the data only inside a secure research environment under controls
connects directly to the underlying database tables to run their own queries
rationale: An API lets the consumer request data programmatically through a defined interface. Receiving a fixed prepared file is a provided extract. Connecting straight to the underlying tables is a direct database connection. Working only inside a secure environment under controls describes querying within a trusted research environment.

stem: Being given a provided extract as an access method means that the consumer:
options: queries the live system themselves through a programmatic interface on demand
is granted a direct connection to the provider's underlying database tables
receives a prepared file or dataset selected and supplied to them by the provider
may analyse the data only within a controlled secure data environment
rationale: A provided extract is a prepared file or dataset the provider selects and supplies. Querying the live system through a programmatic interface is API access. A direct connection to the underlying tables is a direct database connection. Being confined to a controlled environment for analysis is the trusted research environment model.

stem: An arrangement where analysts work on data inside a controlled environment they cannot remove it from, with outputs checked before release, is usually called a:
options: a data sharing agreement or data processing contract
data warehouse or analytical data store
provided extract or data download
Trusted Research Environment or Secure Data Environment
rationale: An environment analysts work inside, cannot remove data from, with outputs checked before release, is a Trusted Research Environment or Secure Data Environment. A data warehouse or analytical store is a storage model, not a controlled access setting. A provided extract or download is precisely data that leaves the provider, the opposite of this. A data sharing agreement is a legal instrument governing transfer, not the controlled environment itself.

stem: A team needs to store scanned consent forms and recordings from a focus group so that each can be retrieved later as a complete file. The most suitable storage model is:
options: a relational database
blob or object storage
a data warehouse
a transactional database
rationale: Whole files such as scanned forms and recordings are best kept as self-contained objects, which is blob or object storage. A relational database holds structured rows linked by keys, not whole files. A data warehouse holds integrated structured data modelled for analysis. A transactional database records a single application's live operations. None of the three suits storing whole files for later retrieval.

stem: An analyst is told they may not remove the data from the provider's system, and that any results they produce will be reviewed before they can take them away. This access arrangement is most consistent with:
options: querying within a secure data environment
receiving a provided extract
a direct database connection
an application programming interface (API)
rationale: Not being allowed to remove data, with outputs reviewed before release, is the secure data environment model. A direct database connection would let the analyst pull data to their own tools. A provided extract is data they take away to work on freely. An API returns data to wherever the analyst requests it. The latter three all let data leave the provider, so none fits the stated controls.

stem: In general terms, interoperability between two separate information systems refers to their ability to:
options: refresh their data on the same fixed schedule at the same time each day
be operated by the same team using one shared set of login credentials
hold their data on the same physical server within a single shared building
exchange data and use it meaningfully, so the combined information makes sense
rationale: Interoperability is the ability of separate systems to exchange data and use it meaningfully together. Sharing a physical server is co-location, not interoperability. Being run by one team with shared logins is an operational arrangement. Refreshing on the same schedule is a matter of cadence, not of exchanging meaning.

stem: A shared or standard vocabulary is valuable when combining data from different systems mainly because it:
options: lets the same real-world thing be recognised as the same across the systems
allows the combined data to be refreshed continuously rather than in batches
ensures that each fact will be stored once across the joined tables
removes the need for either system to record where its data came from
rationale: A shared vocabulary lets the same real-world thing be recognised as the same across systems, which is what makes combination meaningful. It does not remove the need to record provenance. It has nothing to do with refresh cadence. Storing each fact once is a normalisation property of one database, not a benefit of shared vocabulary across systems.

stem: Mapping between two coding schemes is best described as:
options: agreeing a single shared scheme that both systems will adopt instead
combining rows from two tables by matching them on a shared key
setting out which codes in one scheme correspond to which codes in another
translating the free-text labels in one system into a standard spelling
rationale: Mapping establishes which codes in one scheme correspond to which in another. Agreeing a single shared scheme is standardisation, which removes the need to map rather than being mapping itself. Combining rows on a shared key is a database join within one system. Standardising free-text spelling is a cleaning step on labels, not a correspondence between code sets.

stem: A general reason that mapping between two coding schemes can be imperfect is that:
options: the two schemes were published by different organisations
one scheme uses numbers for its codes and the other uses letters
one scheme is stored inside a database and the other inside a spreadsheet
the schemes may have overlapping categories, so some concepts do not line up
rationale: Mapping is imperfect mainly because the schemes may carve up concepts differently, with overlapping categories that do not line up cleanly. The storage medium of each scheme has no bearing on whether codes correspond. Being published by different organisations does not by itself prevent a clean mapping.
