Whether codes are numeric or alphabetic is a surface format difference, not a reason concepts fail to align.

stem: The main practical motivation for getting separate health and care systems to exchange and combine data is to:
options: ensure each system uses an identical schedule for refreshing its data
reduce the total number of physical servers the whole organisation has to run
combine what separate systems each hold about the same people or events
allow each system to be queried using exactly the same access role
rationale: Separate systems are combined so that partial information each holds about the same people or events can be brought together. Reducing the server count is an infrastructure saving, not the motivation for combining meaning. Identical refresh schedules concern cadence. Shared access roles concern who may query, neither of which is the purpose of combining data.

stem: Two registries record the same diagnoses using different code sets, and an analyst finds that several codes in one have no exact equivalent in the other. This situation most directly illustrates:
options: a data quality problem, because one registry must have coded its records wrongly
a loss of provenance, because it is no longer clear which registry a code came from
incomplete harmonisation, because no shared vocabulary has been agreed between them
the imperfection of mapping, because the schemes do not divide concepts identically
rationale: Codes with no exact equivalent across schemes is the classic imperfection of mapping. Incomplete harmonisation is close and tempting, but harmonisation is the broader goal mapping serves; the specific phenomenon here is the imperfect correspondence itself. It is not a data quality problem: both registries may have coded correctly within their own scheme. It is not a loss of provenance, since each code's source registry is still known.

stem: When two systems agree to use a common vocabulary so their data can be combined, the principle being applied is:
options: mapping
harmonisation
normalisation
validation
rationale: Agreeing a common vocabulary so data can be combined is harmonisation. Mapping is the close alternative: it relates one scheme's codes to another's after the fact, rather than agreeing a shared vocabulary up front, which makes it the tempting wrong answer. Normalisation concerns storing each fact once within one database. Validation confirms a dataset is fit for use. Only harmonisation names the agreement on a shared vocabulary.

stem: Treating interoperability as a design principle, rather than as a feature of any single product, means focusing on:
options: whether separate systems can exchange and combine data, however each is built
which single supplier's database the whole organisation should standardise on
how many user roles each individual system defines internally
how often each individual system refreshes its own stored data
rationale: As a design principle, interoperability is about whether separate systems can exchange and combine data meaningfully regardless of how each is built. Choosing one supplier's database is a procurement decision, not the principle. How often a system refreshes is its own cadence. How many roles a system defines is its own access design. None of those is the cross-system exchange of meaning.

stem: Data lineage is best described as a record of:
options: how often the data is refreshed from its originating system
where data came from and how it was transformed into its current form
how long the data will be kept before it is securely deleted
which users are permitted to read or to change the data at each stage
rationale: Lineage records where data came from and how it was transformed to reach its current form. Which users may read or change it is access control. How long it is kept before deletion is retention. How often it refreshes is cadence. Only lineage concerns the origin-and-transformation history of the data.

stem: Saying that a dataset is fit for use is a judgement that it is:
options: of high enough quality to serve any future purpose it might be put to
accessible to every member of staff across the organisation
stored in the most modern storage model currently available
good enough in quality and content for the particular purpose at hand
rationale: Fitness for use judges whether data is good enough for the particular purpose at hand. Being accessible to all staff is an access matter and often undesirable. The storage model is irrelevant to fitness. Being good enough for any future purpose overreaches: fitness is always relative to a specific use, not a guarantee for all uses, which is the tempting but wrong generalisation.

stem: Validation, in the sense used for a dataset, is the activity of:
options: checking that every user has been assigned an appropriate access role
evaluating the sequence of transformations the data has passed through
confirming that a dataset meets defined expectations and is fit to be used
confirming where each record in the dataset was originally sourced from
rationale: Validation confirms a dataset meets defined expectations and is fit to use. Evaluating the sequence of transformations is reviewing lineage, a related but distinct activity. Confirming where each record was sourced is establishing provenance, again neighbouring but not the same. Checking that users have appropriate access roles is an access-control review, not a judgement about the data itself.

stem: In the context of an analysis, version control supports reproducibility mainly by:
options: keeping a copy of the final output in a second location as a backup
recording changes to code and inputs so a result can be regenerated later
recording who approved the analysis before it was published
storing each successive result so the most recent one can always be found
rationale: Version control records changes to code and inputs so a result can be regenerated, which is what supports reproducibility. Storing only the results would not let them be regenerated, since the inputs behind them are not kept. Recording who approved the work is an audit of sign-off, not of inputs. Keeping a backup of the final output protects against loss but does not capture how the output was produced.

stem: Reproducibility of an analysis is the property that:
options: the analysis runs faster each time it is repeated on the same machine
the same conclusion can be reached using different data and a different method
the result can be produced again only by the analyst who originally ran it
the same inputs and method can be rerun by someone else to give the same result
rationale: Reproducibility means the same inputs and method can be rerun, by someone else, to the same result. Reaching the same conclusion from different data and methods is replication, a distinct and often-confused idea. A result only the original analyst can produce is the opposite of reproducible. Running faster on repetition is a performance matter with no bearing on whether the result can be regenerated.

stem: An analyst is deciding whether to rely on a dataset for an important publication. Knowing its provenance helps most because it lets the analyst:
options: work out exactly how the dataset should be split into normalised tables
decide how often the dataset will need to be refreshed in future
see where the data came from and how it was handled, to weigh trust
establish which access roles should be granted over the dataset
rationale: Provenance shows where data came from and how it was handled, letting the analyst judge how far to trust it for the publication. Deciding how to split the data into normalised tables is a structural design task, unrelated to trust. Setting access roles is an access-control decision. Deciding refresh frequency is a cadence question. Only knowing origin and handling speaks to trustworthiness.

stem: A team maintains a dataset that is updated each month, and needs to be able to recover exactly which records and values it contained at an earlier point in time. The capability they need is:
options: a streaming feed, so the dataset is updated continuously rather than monthly
role-based access control, so only approved staff can change the data
a retention schedule, so older data is deleted once it is no longer needed
version control of the dataset, so an earlier state of the data can be recovered
rationale: Recovering exactly what a dataset contained at an earlier point is version control applied to the data itself. A retention schedule deletes old data rather than preserving past states, the opposite of what is needed. Role-based access control governs who may change the data, not whether earlier states can be recovered. A streaming feed changes update frequency but keeps no history of past states.

stem: An analyst is offered a dataset that is broadly accurate but is missing several fields the planned study needs. Judging whether to use it is fundamentally a question of:
options: data retention
reproducibility
data lineage
fitness for use
rationale: Weighing a dataset's content against a study's needs is a fitness-for-use judgement. Data lineage is the record of where the data came from and how it was transformed, which does not settle whether it suits this study. Retention concerns how long to keep the data. Reproducibility concerns whether an analysis can be rerun to the same result. Only fitness for use addresses suitability for the purpose.

stem: Validation and lineage answer different questions about a dataset. Validation asks:
options: does this dataset meet expectations, while lineage asks how recent it is
is this dataset complete, while lineage asks whether it is accurate
is this dataset accurate, while lineage asks whether it is fit to use
is this dataset fit to use, while lineage asks where it came from
rationale: Validation asks whether a dataset is fit to use; lineage asks where it came from and how it changed. The completeness-versus-accuracy split names two quality dimensions but assigns neither to lineage correctly. Meeting expectations is part of validation, but lineage is about origin, not recency. The last option swaps the two ideas, putting fitness under lineage. Only the fit-versus-origin split matches each term to its real question.

stem: Keeping a documented record of how a published output was produced primarily helps because it:
options: allows the result to be checked and reproduced by someone other than its author
removes the need to apply any retention period to the underlying data
means the data no longer needs to be validated before it is used
lets the output be stored as an unstructured object rather than a table
rationale: A documented record of how an output was produced lets others check and reproduce it. It does not remove the need for a retention period, which applies regardless. It has no bearing on whether the output is stored as an object or a table. And it does not replace validation, which confirms fitness before use.

stem: As a system design property, role-based access control (RBAC) grants access on the basis of:
options: a set of attributes such as location, device or time of the request
a credential such as a password or key held by whoever is making the request
the identity of each named individual, with permissions set person by person
the role a user holds, with permissions attached to roles not individuals
rationale: Role-based access control grants access by the role a user holds, with permissions attached to roles. Setting permissions person by person is individual-based access control, the very approach RBAC replaces. Granting on attributes such as location, device or time is attribute-based access control, a different model. Granting on possession of a credential is authentication, which establishes who is asking rather than what their role permits.

stem: The principle of least privilege means that each user is given:
options: the same standard set of access that every other user receives
access to anything not explicitly forbidden to them
access matched to what their task requires, and not beyond it
access decided by how senior they are in the organisation
rationale: Least privilege matches each user's access to what their task requires, and not beyond it. A uniform standard set for everyone ignores what each task actually requires. Granting everything not explicitly forbidden is the opposite default: permissive rather than minimal. Tying access to seniority grants by rank rather than by need, which can give senior staff far more than their task requires.

stem: A system is required to delete records automatically once they reach a set age. The design property this requirement calls for is:
options: retention, expressed as a rule for how long data is kept before disposal
role-based access control, granting access according to a user's role
validation, confirming that the data meets defined expectations
least privilege, limiting each user to the access their task needs
rationale: A rule that deletes records once they reach a set age is a retention property. Least privilege limits how much access each user has, not how long data is kept. Role-based access control decides who may reach the data, again not its lifespan. Validation confirms the data is fit to use. Only retention governs how long data is held before disposal.

stem: Why is role-based access control usually preferred to setting each individual's permissions separately?
options: as people change jobs their access follows the role, not reset by hand
it lets a user hold several different sets of permissions at the same time
it allows access to be granted without anyone needing to approve it first
it makes each individual's permissions independent of everyone else's
rationale: Role-based access control is preferred because access follows the role: when people move jobs their access changes with the role rather than being edited by hand each time. Holding several permission sets at once is not the advantage and is usually avoided. Removing the need for approval is not a property of RBAC and would weaken control. Making each person's permissions wholly independent describes individual-based access, the approach RBAC moves away from.

stem: A new analyst is given access only to the specific tables their project requires, rather than to the whole database. This is the clearest example of:
options: segregation of duties
data minimisation
least privilege
role-based access control
rationale: Confining a user to only the tables their project needs is least privilege. Role-based access control is the close alternative: it is the mechanism by which such limits are often applied, but the principle being illustrated is the minimal grant itself. Data minimisation concerns collecting and keeping no more data than needed, not access scope. Segregation of duties splits a task across people so no one holds total control, which is a different control entirely.

stem: A dissemination platform must ensure that, once a dataset's agreed holding period has passed, the data is removed. The property this refers to is:
options: reproducibility
least privilege
validation
retention
rationale: Keeping data for a set period and then removing it is retention. Least privilege limits how much access each user has, not how long data is kept. Validation confirms a dataset is fit for its purpose. Reproducibility concerns whether an analysis can be rerun to the same result. Only retention covers holding then removing data on a schedule.

stem: Considered as system design properties rather than as a legal framework, RBAC, least privilege and retention are best described as:
options: coding schemes that two separate systems map between in order to exchange data
stages that data passes through on its way from source to use
capabilities a storage and dissemination solution must be able to support
delivery mechanisms by which finished outputs reach their audience
rationale: RBAC, least privilege and retention are capabilities a storage and dissemination solution must support. Coding schemes mapped between systems are an interoperability concept. Stages data passes through are processing stages. Delivery mechanisms for finished outputs are dissemination channels. Only the description as supportable capabilities fits these three as design properties.

stem: If a system can attach permissions to roles but cannot confine users to the minimum access they need, it supports:
options: least privilege but not role-based access control
validation but not retention
role-based access control but not least privilege
retention but not role-based access control
rationale: Attaching permissions to roles is role-based access control; failing to confine users to the minimum needed means least privilege is not enforced, so the system has the former but not the latter. The reverse pairing is the wrong way round. Retention concerns holding periods, not access. Validation concerns fitness for use, not access at all.

stem: In the context of a published output, metadata is best described as:
options: information describing the data: its coverage, production and limitations
the index of earlier editions showing how the output has changed over time
the documented method setting out each step taken to produce the figures
the summary commentary that interprets the main findings for readers
rationale: Metadata is information describing the data: its coverage, how it was produced and its limitations. A documented method setting out each step is methodology, which sits alongside metadata but describes the process rather than the data. Summary commentary interprets findings, which is part of the publication's content, not data description. An index of earlier editions is version history. All three are real companions to a published output, which is what makes them tempting.

stem: Publishing a documented methodology alongside a statistical output mainly serves to:
options: set the fixed period after which the underlying data will be deleted
let users understand how the figures were produced and judge them
decide which storage model the underlying data should sit in
determine the schedule on which the output will be refreshed
rationale: A documented methodology lets users understand how figures were produced and judge them. Setting a deletion period is retention. Choosing a storage model is a technical decision separate from the methodology. Setting a refresh schedule is cadence. Only the documented methodology explains how the output was made.

stem: Applying version control to a published output means that:
options: only the most recent edition is kept and earlier ones are discarded
each successive edition is tracked, so users can tell which they have
the output is re-issued automatically whenever the source data changes
each edition is checked for errors before it is allowed to be released
rationale: Version control of an output tracks successive editions so users can tell which they have. Checking each edition for errors before release is quality assurance, which may happen alongside but is a different activity. Keeping only the latest edition and discarding the rest is the opposite of version control, which preserves the history. Automatic re-issue on data change is a refresh behaviour, not version tracking.

stem: An analytical dataset, as a dissemination artefact, is best described as:
options: a finished set of tables and charts presenting the results of an analysis
a live dashboard letting users explore current figures without downloading them
a written report interpreting the findings for a non-technical audience
a prepared dataset released so that others can carry out their own analysis
rationale: An analytical dataset is data prepared and released so others can run their own analysis. A finished set of tables and charts is a statistical output presenting results, not the underlying data for reanalysis. A written report interprets findings rather than supplying data. A live dashboard offers exploration without giving users the data. All three wrong options are dissemination artefacts, but only an analytical dataset hands over data for others to analyse.

stem: A statistical publication differs from a served data feed mainly in that the publication:
options: updates continuously as new records arrive at its source
presents finished figures and commentary for readers to take in directly
supplies the underlying records for the recipient's own system to process
is tailored to the specific query each recipient sends it
rationale: A statistical publication presents finished figures and commentary for readers to take in directly. Supplying the underlying records for another system to process is exactly what a data feed does, the contrast being drawn. Updating continuously as records arrive describes a live feed, not a fixed publication. Being tailored to each recipient's query describes an interface that responds on demand, again unlike a fixed publication.

stem: A dashboard, as a delivery mechanism, is most appropriate when the audience needs to:
options: read a single fixed written summary of the findings that will never change
receive a formal document they can cite and file as a record
watch and explore a set of current indicators, without handling the data
take away the underlying records to combine with their own data
rationale: A dashboard suits an audience that needs to watch and explore current indicators without handling the data. A single fixed summary that will not change is a static report or publication. Taking away the underlying records to combine elsewhere calls for a data extract or feed. A formal citable document to file is a published report. Each wrong option names a real delivery mechanism better suited to a different need.

stem: When choosing a delivery mechanism, why do its access and permission implications matter?
options: different mechanisms expose different amounts of data, needing different controls
the mechanism decides how often the published figures will get refreshed in future
the mechanism determines how much the data will cost to store
the mechanism fixes the level of detail the analysis can ever reach
rationale: Access and permission implications matter because different mechanisms expose different amounts of data, so each needs its own controls. How often figures refresh is a cadence question set separately from access. Storage cost is a resourcing matter, not an access implication. The level of detail an analysis can reach is set by the data collected, not by the delivery mechanism. Only the exposure-and-control point bears on access and permissions.

stem: An audience needs to monitor a small set of indicators that change daily and wants to explore them themselves without being given the raw records. The most suitable delivery mechanism is:
options: a dashboard, which presents current indicators without exposing the raw records
a one-off statistical publication, which presents fixed figures that do not update
a served data feed, which supplies the raw records for their own systems to process
a direct database connection, which lets them query the underlying tables themselves
rationale: Indicators that change daily, explored interactively without handing over raw records, point to a dashboard. A served data feed would supply the raw records, the opposite of what is wanted. A direct connection would expose the underlying tables. A one-off publication presents fixed figures that do not update daily, so it does not meet the need.

stem: A team wants to release a prepared dataset so that external researchers can run their own analyses on it. The dissemination artefact they are producing is best described as:
options: a dashboard, presenting indicators for interactive viewing
an analytical dataset, released for others to analyse themselves
a statistical publication, presenting finished figures and commentary
a documented methodology, explaining how an output was produced
rationale: A prepared dataset released for others to analyse is an analytical dataset. A dashboard presents indicators for viewing, not a dataset to analyse. A statistical publication presents finished figures and commentary, not raw data for reanalysis. A documented methodology explains how an output was made; it is not itself the dataset.

stem: A published report includes information stating what each field means, the period the data covers and how the figures were derived. This accompanying information is best described as:
options: data lineage internal to the pipeline that produced the output
role-based access control governing who may read the published output
a retention schedule setting when the output will be deleted
metadata and documented methodology supporting the published output
rationale: Information on what fields mean, the coverage and how figures were derived is metadata together with documented methodology. Role-based access control governs who may read the output, not what it describes. Lineage is an internal pipeline record of transformations, not user-facing accompanying information. A retention schedule sets deletion timing, which is not what this information provides.

stem: The continuous period a patient spends in hospital from admission to discharge, however many consultants take responsibility for their care during it, is known as:
options: an inpatient pathway
a finished consultant episode
an attendance
an inpatient spell
rationale: The whole admission-to-discharge stay is a spell, and it can hold several consultant episodes within it. A consultant episode is only the portion of that stay under one named consultant, so it is a part of the spell rather than the whole. An attendance is a non-admitted contact and does not describe an inpatient stay. A pathway is a broader route of care that can span several settings, not the single continuous stay itself.

stem: The period of a hospital stay during which a patient is under the continuous care of one named consultant is called:
options: an attendance
a consultant episode
an inpatient spell
a ward stay
rationale: Care under a single named consultant is a consultant episode, and a stay may contain more than one if responsibility transfers. The full admission-to-discharge stay is a spell, the larger unit that holds the episodes. A ward stay is not a defined activity unit, since a patient can change ward without the responsible consultant changing. An attendance is a non-admitted contact, not a period of inpatient care.

stem: A patient is admitted under a respiratory physician, then responsibility passes to a cardiologist two days later before discharge. Which single stay-and-count description fits?
options: two attendances within one pathway
two spells, each with one consultant episode
one spell made up of two consultant episodes
one spell made up of one consultant episode
rationale: The admission-to-discharge stay is one spell, and because responsible care moved between two named consultants it contains two consultant episodes. Counting one episode ignores the transfer of care. Counting two spells double-counts a single continuous stay. Attendances are non-admitted contacts and do not describe an inpatient stay at all.

stem: An admission that is arranged and booked in advance, rather than arising from an emergency or urgent unplanned need, is described as:
options: elective care
a daycase
non-elective care
ambulatory emergency care
rationale: A planned, booked-ahead admission is elective care. Non-elective care is the opposite, an emergency or urgent unplanned admission. Ambulatory emergency care is a same-day emergency route, so it is unplanned by nature. A daycase describes length of stay, planned same-day admission, which is a separate axis from whether care was planned or unplanned.

stem: A patient arrives at the emergency department acutely unwell and is admitted the same evening for urgent treatment. In activity terms this admission is best classed as:
options: a daycase
an outpatient attendance
elective care
non-elective care
rationale: An urgent, unplanned admission through the emergency route is non-elective care. Elective care would require the admission to have been planned and booked ahead, which this was not. A daycase is a planned same-day admission, again not matching an emergency presentation. An outpatient attendance involves no admission at all, whereas this patient was admitted.

stem: A contact at which a patient is seen and assessed at a clinic without being admitted to a hospital bed is recorded as:
options: an ambulatory emergency care episode
an outpatient attendance
an inpatient spell
a daycase
rationale: A clinic contact with no admission to a bed is an outpatient attendance. A daycase does involve admission to a bed, just without an overnight stay, so it is one step more than an attendance. An inpatient spell is an admitted stay from admission to discharge. Ambulatory emergency care is an emergency same-day route rather than a routine clinic contact.

stem: A planned admission in which the patient occupies a bed but is admitted and discharged on the same day, with no overnight stay, is a:
options: short-stay non-elective admission
outpatient attendance
same day emergency care episode
daycase
rationale: A planned same-day admission that uses a bed without an overnight stay is a daycase. An outpatient attendance uses no bed at all, so it falls short of a daycase. A short-stay non-elective admission is unplanned and emergency-driven, unlike the planned daycase. Same day emergency care is also an emergency route, whereas a daycase is planned in advance.

stem: A recorded contact at an outpatient clinic or emergency department where the patient is not admitted to an inpatient bed is an:
options: attendance
inpatient spell
consultant episode
elective admission
rationale: A non-admitted contact at a clinic or emergency department is an attendance. An inpatient spell is an admitted stay from admission to discharge, the admitted counterpart. A consultant episode is a portion of an admitted stay under one consultant, so it too requires admission. An elective admission is a planned admitted stay, again not a non-admitted contact.

stem: A patient arrives as an emergency, is investigated and treated over a few hours, and is discharged home the same day without ever being admitted to an inpatient bed. Which term best describes this?
options: a daycase
a delayed transfer of care
same day emergency care
an outpatient attendance
rationale: An emergency patient assessed, treated and discharged the same day without inpatient admission is receiving same day emergency care. A daycase is a planned same-day admission, not an emergency presentation, and it does involve a booked bed. An outpatient attendance involves no emergency assessment-and-treatment of this kind. A delayed transfer of care is the opposite situation, a patient ready to leave but unable to, rather than one discharged promptly.

stem: The care model in which emergency patients are managed and sent home the same day without an overnight admission, now most often referred to as same day emergency care, was previously known as:
options: ambulatory emergency care
reablement
intermediate care
elective daycase surgery
rationale: The same-day emergency, admission-avoiding model was previously termed ambulatory emergency care, with same day emergency care now the common label for it. Intermediate care is short-term recovery support after acute illness, not an emergency front-door model. Elective daycase surgery is planned, not emergency, care. Reablement is home-based support to regain independence, a community service rather than an emergency route.

stem: The process of quickly assessing patients on arrival to sort them by clinical urgency and decide the order in which they are seen is:
options: casemix classification
clinical acuity scoring
triage
risk stratification
rationale: Sorting arriving patients by urgency to order who is seen first is triage. Risk stratification groups a whole population by future risk to target care, not arrivals in a queue. Casemix classification groups completed activity by the type and complexity of cases, a coding and funding purpose rather than a sorting-on-arrival one. Clinical acuity scoring rates how unwell an individual is at a point in time, which can feed triage but is not the sorting process itself.

stem: The waiting time measured from a patient's referral to the start of their treatment is known as the:
options: delayed transfer of care period
finished consultant episode
referral to treatment (RTT) waiting time
inpatient spell from admission to discharge
rationale: The time from referral to the start of treatment is the referral to treatment waiting time, tracked by the RTT clock. An inpatient spell measures a stay from admission to discharge, a different interval entirely. A delayed transfer of care period is time a patient waits to leave once ready for discharge, at the end of care rather than before it starts. A consultant episode is a portion of an admitted stay under one consultant, not a referral-to-treatment measure.

stem: A patient returning to hospital as an emergency shortly after being discharged from a previous admission is recorded as a:
options: delayed transfer of care
readmission
non-elective new attendance
transfer of care
rationale: An emergency return soon after discharge is a readmission, often used as an indicator of care quality. A delayed transfer of care is a patient still in hospital who is ready to leave but cannot, not one who has left and come back. A transfer of care is the handover of a patient between services or settings, not a return to hospital. An attendance is a non-admitted contact, whereas a readmission is a fresh admission.

stem: The status of a patient whose acute clinical treatment is complete and who no longer needs a hospital bed on medical grounds, whether or not they have actually left, is:
options: delayed transfer of care
reablement
step-down care
medically fit for discharge
rationale: A patient whose acute treatment is done and who no longer needs a bed on clinical grounds is medically fit for discharge. A delayed transfer of care describes what happens next if such a patient cannot leave, so it is a consequence rather than the status itself. Reablement is a home-based service to regain independence after leaving. Step-down care is a lower-intensity setting a patient may move to, not the clinical-readiness status.

stem: A patient finished acute treatment four days ago and no longer needs a hospital bed on medical grounds, but remains in hospital because a community care package is not yet ready. This ongoing situation is a:
options: readmission
delayed transfer of care
consultant episode
medically fit for discharge status on its own
rationale: A patient who is ready to leave but held in hospital because the next setting is not ready is a delayed transfer of care. A consultant episode is a period of care under a named consultant, not a discharge delay. A readmission is a return to hospital after leaving, the opposite direction of travel. Being medically fit for discharge describes the clinical readiness, but on its own it does not capture the delay caused by the package not being ready, which is the point here.

stem: Conditions for which timely and effective care outside hospital can often prevent the need for an emergency admission, such as some cases of asthma or heart failure, are termed:
options: multimorbid conditions
ambulatory care sensitive conditions
non-elective admissions
ambulatory emergency care presentations
rationale: Conditions where good out-of-hospital care can head off an emergency admission are ambulatory care sensitive conditions, a current term the NHS still uses as a marker of community care quality. This is a separate term from ambulatory emergency care, which is a same-day hospital route for emergencies rather than a class of conditions, so the two should not be confused. A non-elective admission is any unplanned emergency admission, not specifically one that better community care could have avoided. Multimorbidity is the presence of several long-term conditions in one person, a different idea from admission preventability.

stem: The number of new cases of a condition arising in a population over a defined period is measured by its:
options: incidence
prevalence
burden of disease
casemix
rationale: New cases arising over a period are counted by incidence. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or over a period, new and long-standing together, so it captures a different quantity. Burden of disease aggregates the total impact of illness, combining death and disability, rather than counting new cases. Casemix describes the mix of case types and complexity in an activity dataset, not the rate of new disease.

stem: The proportion of a population that has a given condition at a particular point in time, counting both long-standing and recent cases, is its:
options: prevalence
incidence
multimorbidity
avoidable mortality
rationale: All existing cases at a point in time, old and new together, are counted by prevalence. Incidence counts only new cases arising over a period, so it excludes the long-standing ones. Avoidable mortality concerns deaths that could have been prevented, not the proportion currently living with a condition. Multimorbidity is the presence of several conditions in one person, not the population share with a single condition.

stem: For a long-lasting chronic condition where people live for many years after diagnosis, the measure that will be considerably higher than the other, because cases accumulate rather than resolve, is the:
options: attack rate
case fatality
incidence
prevalence
rationale: In a long-lasting condition cases build up in the population, so prevalence rises well above the rate of new cases. Incidence stays comparatively low because it counts new cases each period, regardless of how long people live with the condition. Case fatality is the proportion of cases who die, not a count of existing cases. An attack rate is a form of incidence used in outbreaks, so it too counts new cases rather than accumulated ones.

stem: A report states that on a single survey date, twelve in every hundred adults in an area were living with diagnosed diabetes. This figure is a measure of:
options: incidence
prevalence
burden of disease
risk stratification
rationale: A count of all people living with a condition on a given date is prevalence. Incidence would instead count only new diagnoses arising over a period, not the total living with it. Burden of disease combines mortality and disability into an overall impact measure, not a simple proportion with a condition. Risk stratification sorts a population by future risk, which is not what a point-in-time proportion describes.

stem: Sorting a population into groups according to their likely future risk of poor outcomes, so that care and resources can be targeted at those most likely to need them, is:
options: casemix adjustment
segmentation
risk stratification
triage
rationale: Grouping a population by future risk to target care is risk stratification. Segmentation also divides a population, but by shared characteristics or needs rather than specifically by predicted risk. Triage sorts patients presenting now by immediate clinical urgency, not a population by future risk. Casemix adjustment accounts for the mix of case complexity when comparing activity, a different purpose again.

stem: Dividing a population into groups that share similar characteristics or care needs, in order to design services around each group, is known as:
options: risk stratification
segmentation
triage
multimorbidity
rationale: Grouping a population by shared characteristics or needs to shape services is segmentation. Risk stratification divides by predicted future risk specifically, which is a narrower basis than shared needs generally. Triage sorts individuals presenting now by urgency, not a whole population by shared traits. Multimorbidity describes one person having several conditions, not a way of dividing a population.

stem: A team divides its registered patients into bands representing low, moderate and high likelihood of an unplanned admission in the coming year, so it can offer intensive support to the highest band. This is an example of:
options: risk stratification
triage
segmentation
casemix classification
rationale: Banding a population by predicted future risk to target the highest-risk group is risk stratification. Segmentation would group by shared characteristics or needs rather than specifically by modelled future risk. Casemix classification groups completed activity by case type and complexity, not patients by future risk. Triage orders patients presenting now by immediate urgency, not by a year-ahead risk of admission.

stem: The range and relative complexity of the types of case a service treats, often used when comparing activity or costs fairly between providers, is captured by its:
options: risk stratification
incidence
prevalence
casemix
rationale: The mix and complexity of case types a service handles is its casemix, used to make fair comparisons. Incidence counts new cases of a condition in a population, not the complexity mix of a service's workload. Risk stratification sorts a population by future risk, a forward-looking targeting tool rather than a description of treated activity. Prevalence counts existing cases in a population, again not the complexity profile of a service.

stem: The presence of two or more long-term health conditions in the same individual at the same time is described as:
options: casemix
multimorbidity
comorbidity
health inequality
rationale: Two or more long-term conditions coexisting in one person is multimorbidity, which treats the conditions together without singling one out. Comorbidity frames additional conditions relative to one main index condition, so it centres on a primary diagnosis rather than treating them as equals. Casemix is the complexity mix of a service's caseload, not a state within one person. Health inequality concerns unfair differences in health between groups, not multiple conditions in an individual.

stem: Unfair and avoidable differences in health outcomes between different groups in the population, such as between more and less deprived areas, are termed:
options: avoidable mortality
health inequalities
wider determinants of health
burden of disease
rationale: Unfair, avoidable differences in health between groups are health inequalities. The wider determinants of health are the social and economic factors that drive such differences, which are causes rather than the differences themselves. Avoidable mortality is deaths that could have been prevented, a specific outcome measure rather than a between-group gap. Burden of disease aggregates the overall impact of illness in a population, not the disparity between groups.

stem: Deaths that could have been avoided through good quality healthcare once a condition had developed, such as timely and effective treatment, fall under the treatable component of:
options: burden of disease
preventable mortality
case fatality
avoidable mortality
rationale: Avoidable mortality is the umbrella term covering deaths that could be averted, and its treatable component concerns those avoidable through good healthcare after onset. Preventable mortality is the other component, concerning deaths avoidable by stopping the condition arising in the first place through wider public health action, so it sits before onset rather than after. Case fatality is the proportion of people with a condition who die from it, not a classification of avoidability. Burden of disease aggregates total impact of illness, not specifically deaths that could have been averted.

stem: A combined measure that brings together years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability, to express the total impact of a condition on a population, is its:
options: incidence
prevalence
burden of disease
avoidable mortality
rationale: A measure combining early death and disability into a single total impact is burden of disease. Prevalence counts existing cases at a point in time, without weighting for death or disability. Incidence counts new cases over a period, again a simple count rather than a combined impact measure. Avoidable mortality concerns deaths that could have been averted, so it addresses one part of impact rather than the whole death-plus-disability total.

stem: The social, economic and environmental conditions in which people live, such as housing, income, education and employment, which shape health outside of healthcare itself, are the:
options: clinical risk factors
wider determinants of health
health inequalities
indices of deprivation
rationale: The social and economic conditions shaping health beyond healthcare are the wider determinants of health. Indices of deprivation are tools that measure and rank deprivation using such factors, so they are a measurement instrument rather than the conditions themselves. Health inequalities are the unfair differences in outcomes that the determinants help produce, an effect rather than the underlying conditions. Clinical risk factors are individual biological or behavioural characteristics, a narrower category than the broad social determinants.

stem: A tool that combines several domains, such as income, employment, education and housing, to produce an overall ranking of how deprived small areas are relative to one another is an:
options: measure of health inequality
incidence rate
index of deprivation
casemix index
rationale: A composite tool ranking small areas by combined deprivation domains is an index of deprivation. A measure of health inequality captures a gap in outcomes between groups, not a ranking of areas by deprivation. An incidence rate counts new cases of a condition, unrelated to area-level deprivation ranking. A casemix index summarises the complexity of a service's caseload, a different kind of index entirely.

stem: The English Index of Multiple Deprivation combines several weighted domains such as income, employment and education. Which of the following is not one of the domains that make up the IMD?
options: deprivation relating to barriers to housing and services
the ethnic composition of the area's residents
deprivation relating to health and disability
deprivation relating to crime
rationale: The IMD is built from domains including income, employment, education, health and disability, crime, barriers to housing and services, and living environment, so the ethnic composition of an area is not one of them, and deprivation is measured without reference to ethnicity. Crime is one of the seven domains. Health and disability is one of the seven domains. Barriers to housing and services is one of the seven domains. The task is to spot the factor that does not feed into the index.

stem: An analyst notes that a patient lives in an area ranked among the most deprived and concludes the patient must personally be deprived. The flaw is that the Index of Multiple Deprivation measures:
options: the average income of the individuals living in the area, so a high deprivation rank means that every resident must have a low income
the personal deprivation of each named resident, so the area rank can simply be read straight off as any one individual's circumstances
the number of deprived individuals living in the area, so it counts affected people rather than ranking the place against others
the relative deprivation of a small area as a whole, so individual residents may be more or less deprived than the area's rank suggests
rationale: The IMD ranks small areas by relative deprivation, so an individual in a deprived area may be better or worse off than the area's rank implies, which is the analyst's error. It does not measure each resident's personal deprivation, so the rank cannot be read straight off as an individual's circumstances. It is not simply an average income measure, since it combines several weighted domains rather than income alone. It does not count deprived individuals; it produces a relative ranking of the area itself.

stem: Areas in England are grouped into deprivation deciles, with decile 1 being the most deprived tenth. What does it mean to say a neighbourhood is in the most deprived decile?
options: it is among the tenth of neighbourhoods in England with the highest relative deprivation
a tenth of the people living in that neighbourhood are themselves classed as deprived
its overall deprivation score is roughly ten times the national average score
one in ten of its residents falls into the most deprived group in the country
rationale: Deprivation deciles rank neighbourhoods against all others in England, so the most deprived decile is the tenth of neighbourhoods with the highest relative deprivation. It does not mean a tenth of that neighbourhood's people are deprived, since the decile ranks the area against others rather than describing a share of its residents. It does not mean the score is ten times the average, since a decile is a rank band, not a multiple of a score. It does not mean one in ten residents falls in the most deprived national group, which again confuses a share of people with a ranking of the place.

stem: An area's Index of Multiple Deprivation score and rank are best understood as a measure of:
options: the change in the area's deprivation compared with its own score in the previous release of the index
how deprived the area is relative to all other areas in England, rather than an absolute amount of deprivation
the proportion of the area's own residents who are living in poverty at the given point in time being measured
the absolute level of deprivation in the area, measured on a fixed scale that does not depend on any other areas
rationale: The IMD is a relative measure, so a score and rank place an area against all other areas in England rather than giving an absolute quantity of deprivation. It is not an absolute figure on a fixed scale, since the whole index is built to compare areas with one another. It is not a straightforward poverty headcount of residents, since it combines several weighted domains rather than counting people in poverty. It is not a change measure against a previous release, since a rank describes position now rather than movement over time.

stem: An area is described as being in deprivation decile 1. Taking the usual convention that decile 1 is the most deprived tenth, this tells you the area is:
options: among the tenth most deprived areas in the ranking
among the tenth least deprived areas in the ranking
of exactly average deprivation for the country
one where disease incidence is highest
rationale: Under the usual convention decile 1 is the most deprived tenth, so the area sits among the most deprived. Reading it as the least deprived tenth inverts the convention. An average-deprivation area would fall in the middle deciles, not decile 1. Deprivation decile ranks deprivation, not disease incidence, so it does not by itself tell you where incidence is highest.

stem: When a team attributes much of the health gap between two neighbourhoods to differences in housing quality, employment and income rather than to differences in medical treatment, they are pointing to the role of:
options: differences in clinical acuity between the two neighbourhoods
differences in comorbidity between patients in the two neighbourhoods
the wider determinants of health
differences in the casemix treated across the two neighbourhoods
rationale: Attributing a health gap to housing, employment and income points to the wider determinants of health, the social and economic drivers of outcomes. Clinical acuity is how unwell an individual patient is at a moment, not a neighbourhood-level social factor. Casemix is the complexity mix of a service's caseload, unrelated to social conditions between neighbourhoods. Comorbidity concerns additional conditions alongside a main diagnosis in a patient, not the social causes of a population health gap.

stem: A recorded clinical decision that cardiopulmonary resuscitation should not be attempted if a particular patient's heart or breathing stops is a:
options: clinical acuity rating
DNACPR decision
delayed transfer of care
frailty assessment
rationale: A recorded decision not to attempt CPR at cardiac or respiratory arrest is a DNACPR decision. A delayed transfer of care is a discharge delay, unrelated to resuscitation decisions. A frailty assessment gauges a patient's overall vulnerability and decline, not a specific resuscitation instruction. A clinical acuity rating measures how acutely unwell a patient is, which may inform care but is not a decision about CPR.

stem: A patient has a DNACPR decision in place and a relative worries this means treatments such as antibiotics or pain relief will now be withheld. The correct understanding is that a DNACPR decision:
options: automatically classifies the patient as being at the end of life and dying imminently
transfers responsibility for the patient entirely to the palliative care team
withdraws all active medical treatment, including antibiotics and pain relief, from that point onward
applies to attempting cardiopulmonary resuscitation and does not stop other appropriate treatment
rationale: A DNACPR decision concerns whether CPR is attempted, and other appropriate treatments continue as normal. Reading it as withdrawing all treatment overstates it well beyond resuscitation. It does not by itself declare a patient to be at end of life, which is a separate clinical judgement. It does not in itself hand care to palliative services, which would be a distinct referral.

stem: A state of increased vulnerability arising from a decline across several body systems, in which a minor illness or event can trigger a large deterioration in a person's health, is:
options: multimorbidity
comorbidity
clinical acuity
frailty
rationale: Reduced reserve across body systems, where a small event causes a large deterioration, is frailty. Comorbidity is the presence of additional conditions alongside a main diagnosis, which is about disease count rather than overall reserve. Clinical acuity is how acutely unwell someone is at a moment, a snapshot of severity rather than a background state of vulnerability. Multimorbidity is having several long-term conditions, which often accompanies frailty but is not the same as reduced physiological reserve.

stem: A measure of how severely unwell a patient is at a given moment, and therefore how much immediate clinical attention and resource they require, is their:
options: frailty
comorbidity
clinical acuity
casemix
rationale: How acutely unwell a patient is right now, driving immediate care needs, is clinical acuity. Frailty is a longer-standing state of reduced reserve, not a snapshot of current severity. Comorbidity is the presence of additional diagnoses, which is about the burden of conditions rather than momentary severity. Casemix is the complexity mix of a whole service's caseload, not an individual patient's current severity.

stem: An older patient with longstanding reduced physiological reserve arrives with a mild infection but is currently stable and not acutely unwell. The term describing their background vulnerability, as distinct from how unwell they are at this moment, is:
options: readmission risk
clinical acuity
frailty
comorbidity
rationale: The background state of reduced reserve, separate from present severity, is frailty. Clinical acuity would describe how unwell the patient is at this moment, which the situation says is low, so it captures the wrong axis. Comorbidity concerns additional diagnoses rather than a state of vulnerability. Readmission risk is the likelihood of returning to hospital after discharge, not a description of background reserve.

stem: The presence of one or more additional conditions occurring alongside a primary condition that is the main focus of care is termed:
options: frailty
multimorbidity
casemix
comorbidity
rationale: Additional conditions accompanying a main index condition are comorbidity, framed around that primary diagnosis. Multimorbidity treats several coexisting conditions together without singling one out as primary, so it differs in framing. Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve, not a count of accompanying conditions. Casemix is the complexity profile of a service's caseload, not conditions within one patient.

stem: The feature that distinguishes multimorbidity from comorbidity is that multimorbidity:
options: considers several coexisting long-term conditions together without designating one as the primary condition
frames the additional conditions in relation to one main condition that is the focus of care
always involves a greater number of separate conditions than comorbidity does in the very same patient
refers to the pattern of conditions across a whole population rather than within a single individual
rationale: Multimorbidity considers coexisting conditions together with no single index condition, which is what sets it apart from comorbidity. It is not defined by a higher count of conditions; the difference is framing, not number. Both terms describe conditions within an individual, not a population, so shifting to population level misstates it. Framing the additional conditions around one main condition is the description of comorbidity itself, so it is the inverse of what the stem asks for.

stem: A standardised aggregate score based on routine physiological measurements such as pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature, used to flag patients who may be deteriorating, is:
options: a frailty index
NEWS2
a clinical acuity band
a casemix score
rationale: An aggregate of routine vital signs used to detect deterioration is NEWS2, the National Early Warning Score. A frailty index summarises accumulated deficits to gauge vulnerability, not current vital signs. A clinical acuity band is a broad categorisation of how unwell a patient is, not this specific vital-signs aggregate. A casemix score summarises caseload complexity, unrelated to bedside physiological monitoring.

stem: A nurse records a rising NEWS2 score for a patient and a colleague assumes this score names the underlying diagnosis. The correct understanding is that NEWS2:
options: signals the degree of physiological disturbance and prompts escalation, without identifying the cause
removes the need for any further clinical assessment once a given escalation threshold is reached
measures the patient's long-term frailty and background reserve rather than their current state
provides a specific underlying diagnosis based on the particular pattern of the vital signs recorded
rationale: NEWS2 flags the size of physiological disturbance and triggers escalation, but it does not tell you the cause, which the colleague misunderstands. It does not yield a diagnosis, since it aggregates vital signs rather than identifying disease. It reflects the current state, not long-term frailty, so it is not a reserve measure. It supports rather than replaces clinical assessment, which remains necessary at any score.

stem: On a ward, a set of worsening vital-sign observations is combined into a single rising number that triggers a call for urgent senior review. The tool producing that number is:
options: NEWS2
a frailty score
a clinical acuity assessment
a triage category
rationale: A single aggregate of worsening vital signs that triggers escalation is NEWS2. A triage category sorts patients by urgency on arrival rather than tracking an inpatient's vital signs over time. A clinical acuity assessment judges overall severity but is not this specific aggregated vital-signs number. A frailty score gauges background vulnerability, not a real-time deterioration signal from observations.

stem: A patient admitted primarily for treatment of heart failure also has longstanding type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis that are being managed alongside. In relation to the heart failure admission, the diabetes and arthritis are best described as:
options: comorbidities
the primary diagnosis
ambulatory care sensitive conditions
acute presentations
rationale: Additional longstanding conditions managed alongside the main reason for admission are comorbidities relative to that primary diagnosis. Calling them acute presentations misreads longstanding stable conditions as new emergencies. They are not the primary diagnosis, since heart failure is the main focus of this admission. Ambulatory care sensitive conditions is a class of conditions where good community care can prevent admission, which is a different framing from a patient's accompanying diagnoses.

stem: The most accurate understanding of frailty is that it is:
options: a temporary reduction in physical fitness that resolves fully once the acute illness passes
a condition that people inevitably develop once they pass a fixed chronological age threshold
a direct synonym for having several separately diagnosed long-term conditions at once
a state of reduced physiological reserve that is related to but not the same as chronological age
rationale: Frailty is a state of reduced reserve that correlates with age but is not determined by it, so younger people can be frail and older people need not be. It is not something everyone acquires at a set age, since it varies between individuals. It is not simply having several conditions, which is multimorbidity, a related but distinct idea. It is not merely a passing dip in fitness during illness, since it describes a more enduring underlying vulnerability.

stem: Short-term care provided to help a person recover and regain independence after illness or a hospital stay, so as to avoid an unnecessary admission or support a safe discharge, is:
options: social prescribing
reablement
intermediate care
a delayed transfer of care
rationale: Short-term, time-limited care that supports recovery and independence around a hospital stay is intermediate care. Reablement is one specific approach within that broad idea, focused on actively relearning daily tasks, so it is narrower than intermediate care as a whole. Social prescribing connects people to non-clinical community activities, not recovery-focused care after illness. A delayed transfer of care is a discharge delay, not a form of recovery support.

stem: A form of support focused on actively helping a person relearn how to carry out daily activities for themselves, so they regain independence rather than having tasks done for them, is:
options: reablement
step-down care
social prescribing
ordinary domiciliary care
rationale: Support aimed at relearning daily tasks to regain independence is reablement, which is deliberately active rather than doing things for the person. Ordinary domiciliary care tends to do tasks for the person on an ongoing basis, the opposite emphasis to reablement. Step-down care is a lower-intensity setting a patient moves to after acute care, defined by setting rather than the relearning goal. Social prescribing links people to community activities, not daily-living relearning.

stem: A discharge team wants a service whose defining aim is to actively coach a patient to relearn washing, dressing and cooking for themselves, rather than simply providing a period of general recovery support. The service that specifically fits this active-relearning aim is:
options: a social prescribing referral
step-down care
reablement
intermediate care in general
rationale: The service defined by actively coaching relearning of daily tasks is reablement. Intermediate care in general is the broader category of short-term recovery support, of which reablement is the more specific, relearning-focused form. Step-down care describes moving to a lower-intensity setting, not the active-relearning aim. A social prescribing referral connects the patient to community activities, which does not match the daily-living coaching described.

stem: Care provided in a lower-intensity setting to which a patient moves once they no longer need acute hospital care but are not yet ready to go straight home, is:
options: reablement
ambulatory emergency care
step-down care
intermediate care
rationale: A lower-intensity setting bridging acute care and home is step-down care, defined by the move down a level of intensity. Intermediate care is the broader recovery-support category; step-down is one route within that landscape, distinguished by the setting change. Reablement is defined by its active-relearning goal, not by moving to a less intensive setting. Ambulatory emergency care is a same-day emergency route at the hospital front door, the opposite end of the pathway.

stem: A colleague asks how step-down care relates to intermediate care. The most accurate answer is that step-down care:
options: is a wholly separate service that sits entirely outside the intermediate care landscape and is unrelated to it
is simply another name for reablement, sharing the same active-relearning goal under a different label
refers to gradually reducing the intensity of a patient's medication rather than moving their care setting
is one part of the broader intermediate care landscape, describing a move to a less intensive setting after acute care
rationale: Step-down care sits within the broader intermediate care landscape, describing the move to a less intensive setting after acute treatment. Treating it as wholly unrelated to intermediate care misses that it is part of the same recovery landscape. It is not simply reablement renamed, since reablement is defined by active relearning rather than a change of setting. It concerns the level of care setting, not a reduction in medication.

stem: A scheme in which a link worker connects a patient to non-clinical community activities and sources of support, such as exercise groups, befriending or debt advice, to improve wellbeing, is:
options: social prescribing
risk stratification
reablement
intermediate care
rationale: Connecting people to non-clinical community support to improve wellbeing is social prescribing. Reablement is active support to relearn daily living tasks, a clinical-recovery aim rather than a community-connection one. Intermediate care is short-term recovery care around a hospital stay, not linkage to community activities. Risk stratification sorts a population by future risk and does not describe connecting individuals to community support.

stem: A GP judges that a patient's low mood is driven largely by isolation and financial worry, and refers them to a link worker for community groups and debt advice rather than starting medication. This referral is an example of:
options: reablement
social prescribing
step-down care
a non-elective referral
rationale: Referring a patient to non-clinical community support for social drivers of ill health is social prescribing. Reablement would involve actively helping the patient relearn daily living tasks, which is not what the referral provides. Step-down care is a move to a lower-intensity care setting after acute care, unrelated to community support for isolation. A non-elective referral concerns emergency admission, which does not fit a planned community referral.

stem: After a hospital stay a patient is placed for two weeks in a community unit that provides a lower level of care than the acute ward, to continue recovering before going home. This service is best described as:
options: reablement
social prescribing
step-down care
a daycase
rationale: A short placement in a lower-intensity community unit to continue recovery after acute care is step-down care. Reablement is defined by active relearning of daily tasks, not by the placement in a less intensive setting described here. Social prescribing connects people to community activities, not a residential recovery placement. A daycase is a planned same-day hospital admission, unrelated to a two-week recovery placement.

stem: The feature that distinguishes reablement from ordinary ongoing home care is that reablement:
options: works with the person to rebuild their ability to do tasks themselves, aiming to reduce their need for support over time
is delivered only as an inpatient service in a hospital setting rather than in the person's own home
carries on providing the same fixed set of tasks indefinitely, with no aim of reducing the support given over time
connects the person to non-clinical community groups and activities instead of providing hands-on personal care
rationale: Reablement is distinguished by its active aim to rebuild the person's own ability and reduce their need for support over time. Ordinary home care tends to provide tasks on an ongoing basis without that reduction aim, which is the contrast being drawn. Reablement is typically delivered in the person's own home, not confined to hospital. Connecting people to community groups describes social prescribing, not the personal-care relearning of reablement.

stem: A practice employs a link worker whose role is to spend time understanding patients' non-medical needs and connect them to local services and activities. This role is the central feature of:
options: intermediate care
reablement
triage
social prescribing
rationale: A link worker connecting patients to non-medical local services and activities is the central feature of social prescribing. Reablement centres on active relearning of daily tasks, not linkage to community services. Intermediate care provides short-term recovery care around a hospital stay, not the community-connection role of a link worker. Triage sorts patients by clinical urgency on arrival, a wholly different function.

stem: In a discharge pathway, a bed used to take patients who are ready to leave the acute ward but need a further period of lower-intensity care before home is best termed a:
options: delayed transfer of care
reablement placement
step-down bed
social prescribing referral
rationale: A bed taking patients down from acute care to a lower-intensity setting before home is a step-down bed. A reablement placement is defined by active relearning of daily tasks, not simply a lower-intensity bed. A social prescribing referral connects a person to community activities, not a care bed. A delayed transfer of care is a patient stuck in hospital when ready to leave, which describes a problem rather than a planned step-down bed.

stem: A defining feature of intermediate care, distinguishing it from ongoing long-term care, is that it is:
options: available only to patients who are still admitted on an acute hospital ward
provided on an open-ended basis, continuing for as long as the person wishes to receive it
focused on connecting people to community activities and groups rather than on recovery
time-limited, provided for a short defined period with the aim of maximising independence
rationale: Intermediate care is time-limited, given for a short defined period to maximise independence, which sets it apart from ongoing long-term care. It is not provided indefinitely, since its short duration is central to the concept. It is delivered around and after a hospital stay rather than only on the acute ward itself. Connecting people to community activities describes social prescribing, not the recovery focus of intermediate care.

stem: A local authority is coordinating a multi-agency response to concerns about a child's welfare. The statutory guidance that governs how the agencies should work together in this case is:
options: the Care Act 2014
the Data Protection Act 2018
Working Together to Safeguard Children
the Mental Capacity Act 2005
rationale: Working Together to Safeguard Children is the statutory guidance for multi-agency work where a child's welfare is in question. The Care Act 2014 sets the equivalent duties for adults with care and support needs, not children. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs decisions for people who lack capacity, which is a different question again. The Data Protection Act 2018 governs the handling of personal data, not the safeguarding response itself. Each is real legislation in this landscape, so the candidate has to match the child multi-agency case to the guidance that covers it.

stem: The principal statutory basis for safeguarding an adult with care and support needs who is at risk of abuse or neglect is:
options: the Health and Social Care Act 2012
the Care Act 2014
the Equality Act 2010
the Mental Capacity Act 2005
rationale: The Care Act 2014 places the safeguarding duties in respect of adults at risk. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs decision-making for people who lack capacity, which can be relevant but is not the safeguarding basis itself. The Health and Social Care Act 2012 concerns the structure and commissioning of health services. The Equality Act 2010 concerns discrimination and protected characteristics. Each is real legislation an analyst might encounter, so the candidate must identify the one that carries adult safeguarding duties.

stem: The Prevent duty is concerned specifically with:
options: protecting adults at risk from abuse and neglect
reducing the risk of people being drawn into terrorism or supporting it
coordinating the response to high-risk domestic abuse
safeguarding and promoting the welfare of children in need
rationale: Prevent is the duty to have regard to the need to stop people being drawn into terrorism. The adult-abuse option describes Care Act 2014 safeguarding. The high-risk domestic abuse option describes what a MARAC coordinates. The children's welfare option describes the aim of Working Together. Each is a genuine safeguarding function in this KSB, so the candidate must know what marks Prevent out from the others.

stem: An analyst notices that a data record concerns an 82 year old living alone who appears to be at risk of neglect by a paid carer. In terms of the relevant safeguarding regime, this situation falls primarily under:
options: the remit of the Local Authority Designated Officer
the decision-making provisions of the Mental Capacity Act 2005
the Prevent duty
the adult safeguarding duties of the Care Act 2014
rationale: An adult at risk of neglect engages Care Act 2014 adult safeguarding. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs decisions where a person lacks capacity, which may or may not apply here and is not the safeguarding basis itself. Prevent concerns radicalisation, which is not what the scenario describes. The Local Authority Designated Officer deals with allegations against people who work with children, which does not fit an older adult. The candidate has to route the subject to the correct regime rather than the most familiar-sounding one.

stem: A specified authority's obligation under the Prevent duty is best understood as:
options: a statutory duty to have due regard to the need to prevent people being drawn into terrorism
a duty triggered once a criminal offence has been identified
an obligation that applies to individual practitioners rather than to the organisation
a discretionary programme an organisation may adopt if it chooses to
rationale: Prevent is a statutory duty on specified authorities to have due regard to stopping radicalisation. Describing it as discretionary is wrong: it is a legal duty, not an opt-in. Placing it on individuals rather than the organisation misstates where the duty sits. Tying it to an identified criminal offence is wrong because Prevent is about earlier risk, before offending. The three wrong readings are the common misconceptions about the duty's status.

stem: In local safeguarding arrangements, the distinction between the national statutory framework and local procedures is that:
options: local procedures set the specific duties that apply, while national guidance provides the broad framework and processes to follow
national guidance sets the duties and expectations, while local procedures set out who to contact and the steps to follow in that area
national guidance and local procedures are alternative routes, and an employee may follow whichever they prefer
local procedures override national guidance where the two differ on a duty
rationale: National statutory guidance sets the duties; local procedures translate them into named contacts and steps for the area, which is where 'who to contact for advice' is found. The inverted option wrongly puts the specific duties in local procedure and the framework in national guidance. The override option is wrong because local procedure implements rather than overrides statutory duty. The alternative-routes option is wrong because the two are layered, not interchangeable. The candidate must grasp how the national and local levels relate.

stem: The main function of a Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub (MASH) is to:
options: handle allegations made against people who work with children
bring agencies together to share information and triage incoming safeguarding referrals
agree a safety plan for victims at high risk of domestic abuse
take lead responsibility for safeguarding within a single organisation
rationale: A MASH brings agencies together to pool information and triage referrals. Taking lead responsibility within one organisation describes a Designated Safeguarding Lead. Handling allegations against people who work with children describes the LADO. Agreeing a safety plan for high-risk domestic abuse describes a MARAC. Each is a real safeguarding function in this KSB, so the candidate must know which body does which job rather than reading it off the grammar.

stem: The Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO) is the point of contact specifically for:
options: allegations that a person who works with children may have harmed a child or poses a risk to children
concerns that a child in the community is being neglected or abused by a family member
coordinating support for the highest-risk victims of domestic abuse
decisions about how a patient's confidential information may be used
rationale: The LADO handles allegations against adults who work with children. A concern about a child harmed by a family member is a general safeguarding referral, routed to the MASH or children's social care, not the LADO. Confidential-information decisions sit with a Caldicott Guardian. High-risk domestic abuse coordination is a MARAC function. The candidate must separate allegations against staff from safeguarding concerns about children in general.

stem: A Multi-Agency Risk Assessment Conference (MARAC) exists to:
options: triage the full range of incoming safeguarding referrals for an area
bring agencies together to share information and agree a plan for victims at high risk of domestic abuse
advise an organisation on the lawful use of patient confidential information
take lead responsibility for safeguarding arrangements within a single organisation
rationale: A MARAC is the multi-agency forum for the highest-risk domestic abuse cases. Triaging the full range of referrals describes a MASH. Advising on confidential information describes a Caldicott Guardian. Taking lead responsibility within one organisation describes a Designated Safeguarding Lead. Each is a real function in this KSB, and the candidate has to fix the MARAC on high-risk domestic abuse specifically.

stem: Within an organisation, the role held by a Caldicott Guardian is to:
options: triage multi-agency safeguarding referrals as they come in
safeguard the confidentiality and appropriate use of patient information and advise on lawful sharing
manage allegations made against staff who work with children
chair the multi-agency response to high-risk domestic abuse
