works effectively and largely self-manages, with energy focused on the task rather than on internal friction
is openly working through conflict over roles and priorities
has agreed its ways of working but has not yet delivered much
rationale: In the performing stage a team works effectively and can largely manage itself, with its energy going into the task rather than into internal friction. A team just coming together and working out purpose and roles is at the forming stage. A team openly working through conflict is storming. And a team that has agreed its ways of working but not yet delivered much is around the norming stage, one step before performing.

stem: In a team context, team dynamics refers to:
options: the combined technical skills the members individually bring to the work
the formal division of tasks and responsibilities across the team
the patterns of interaction, influence and cohesion that shape how members work together
the seniority ranking that decides whose view carries most weight
rationale: Team dynamics are the patterns of interaction, influence and cohesion that shape how members work together. The combined technical skills members bring are individual inputs, not the pattern of interaction between them. The formal division of tasks is the team's structure rather than its dynamics. And a seniority ranking that decides whose view counts is a formal or hierarchical matter, not the emergent way the team actually works together.

stem: Which of the following is most likely to undermine healthy team dynamics?
options: a few members dominating discussion so that others stop contributing
members sometimes working alone before bringing their parts together
open disagreement about the best way forward before deciding
a tight deadline that puts the whole team under time pressure
rationale: A few members dominating so that others fall silent is the clearest underminer here, because the team loses everyone else's contribution and the cohesion that depends on broad participation. Open disagreement before deciding looks disruptive but is usually a sign of a healthy team, provided it is handled well. Members working alone at times before combining their work is a normal part of how teams operate, not a threat to their dynamics. A tight deadline can add strain, but time pressure affects any team and is not in itself a breakdown in how members work together, unlike a pattern of domination that silences people.

stem: Belbin team roles describe:
options: a fixed personality type that stays the same across every situation
the formal job or functional role each member holds, such as analyst or manager
the technical skills and expertise each member brings to the work
the characteristic ways individuals tend to contribute to a team, such as coordinating, shaping ideas or finishing work
rationale: Belbin team roles describe the characteristic ways people tend to contribute to a team, such as coordinating others, shaping ideas or seeing work through to completion. They are not the formal job or functional role someone holds, such as analyst or manager, which is a position rather than a behavioural contribution. They are not a fixed personality type either: Belbin describes how people tend to behave in a team, which can shift with the team and the task, rather than a trait fixed for all time. And they are not the technical skills a member brings, which are about what someone can do rather than how they tend to contribute to the group.

stem: A team is full of people who are good at generating ideas and pushing them forward, but the work keeps stalling because no one attends to the details or sees tasks through to the finish. In Belbin's terms, the team is short of:
options: a shaping role, to drive the ideas forward more forcefully
another idea-generating role, to add still more options
a completer-finisher role, focused on detail and following through to the end
a coordinating role, to allocate the ideas among members
rationale: The team generates plenty of ideas but nothing gets finished, which points to a gap in the completer-finisher role, the contribution focused on detail and seeing work through. Adding another idea-generating role would deepen the surplus the team already has, not fix the gap. A coordinating role helps organise contributions but does not itself supply the follow-through that is missing. And a shaping role drives ideas forward with energy, which the team already has in abundance, so more of it would not address the failure to finish.

stem: In terms of how teams develop, why do they typically not perform at their best as soon as they are formed?
options: members first need time to build up the technical skills the work demands
they usually lack clear goals and direction until leadership provides them
new teams are typically under-resourced when they start, which holds them back
they need to work through earlier stages, including surfacing and resolving conflict, before they can perform effectively
rationale: In terms of team development, teams usually pass through earlier stages, forming and then storming and norming, working through conflict and settling how they operate, before they reach the performing stage. A lack of clear goals can certainly hold a new team back, but that is a matter of direction rather than the team's own development. Time to build technical skills can matter too, yet the development model is about how members come to work together, not their individual skill level. And limited resources can slow any team, but that is a practical constraint rather than the developmental reason the question asks about.
